docs.title: Accounting — Chart of Accounts, GL, Invoicing, Payments, Tax
What it does
docs.text: Accounting is the module every other module posts into. Selling books revenue, Buying books cost, Stock books value — and all of it lands in the same General Ledger. If the ledger is wrong, the business's numbers are wrong, no matter how good the rest of the ERP looks.

docs.title: Core DocTypes
docs.text: DocType What it is Company The legal entity. Every transaction posts to one Company and one Cost Center. Chart of Accounts / Account The tree of accounts: Asset, Liability, Equity, Income, Expense. Sales Invoice Bills a customer. On submit it books revenue + tax and creates the receivable. Purchase Invoice Books a supplier bill. On submit it creates the payable. Payment Entry Records money in or out, against invoices (or as an advance). Journal Entry Manual adjustments between accounts — corrections, opening balances, accruals. GL Entry One ledger line. Created automatically on submit — never insert it by hand. Cost Center Where money belongs (branch, department, project). Every transaction needs one. Sales Taxes and Charges Template The tax rules applied to a sales invoice (e.g. Sales Tax 18%). Purchase Taxes and Charges Template The same for purchase invoices. Mode of Payment Cash, bank, cheque, card — how the money moved.

docs.title: End-to-end flow
docs.text:
Setup:  Company → Chart of Accounts → Tax Templates → Cost Centers
Sell:   Sales Invoice (submit) → GL Entry: Dr Customer, Cr Income + Tax
Pay:    Payment Entry against the invoice → GL Entry: Dr Bank, Cr Customer
Buy:    Purchase Invoice (submit) → GL Entry: Dr Expense/Stock, Cr Supplier
Pay:    Payment Entry against the invoice → GL Entry: Dr Supplier, Cr Bank
Fix:    Journal Entry for anything that is not an invoice or a payment
Check:  General Ledger, Trial Balance, Balance Sheet, Profit & Loss reports

Two rules run the whole module:

  1. Business state changes only through submit / cancel. To correct a submitted invoice, cancel it and amend it. Never edit its fields, and never write GL Entry rows directly.
  2. Balances come from the ledger reports, not from summing GL Entry in code and never from a document's own totals after submit.

docs.title: Worked example — a trading company, one day
docs.text:
Al-Noor Traders sells 100 cartons of cooking oil to a retailer:

  1. Sales Invoice for Rs 500,000 + 18% sales tax (Rs 90,000). Submit. Ledger: Dr Customer 590,000 — Cr Sales Income 500,000 — Cr Sales Tax Payable 90,000. The customer now owes 590,000.
  2. The retailer pays Rs 300,000 by bank transfer. Payment Entry against the invoice. Ledger: Dr Bank 300,000 — Cr Customer 300,000. Balance outstanding: 290,000.
  3. The company buys 200 cartons from its supplier: Purchase Invoice for Rs 400,000 + tax. Ledger: Dr Stock/Expense 400,000 — Cr Supplier.
  4. Month end: the accountant opens Trial Balance (debits = credits), Profit & Loss (income − expense), and Balance Sheet — all read from the same ledger, so they agree with each other by construction.

docs.title: A real use case
docs.text:
A Lahore distributor was invoicing in Excel and keeping the bank in a separate register. Month-end took a week and the tax return was always an estimate. After moving invoicing and payments into ERPNext, the Sales Tax Payable account showed the exact liability at any moment, and the return was filed from the General Ledger report.

How we can use it: sell Accounting as the first module in every implementation — even a client who "only wants stock" needs the ledger, and the tax template setup (Sales Tax, withholding) is a fixed-price service we can repeat for every Pakistani client.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Posting to the wrong Company or Cost Center. A document without the right company posts to the wrong books. Set the default Company per user and check it on the first invoice of every implementation.
  • Editing a submitted invoice. Cancel and amend. An edited submitted document and its ledger will disagree forever.
  • Inserting GL Entry rows in code. The ledger is the system's memory. If a posting is missing, the document that should have created it is wrong — fix the document, not the ledger.
  • One bank account for everything. Separate accounts per bank (and per currency) or reconciliation becomes guesswork.
  • Tax as a manual line. Use the tax templates. A typed tax amount is wrong the first time the rate changes.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: 02 — Stock & Inventory — where the goods are, and what they are worth.

docs.title: Stock & Inventory — Warehouses, Batches, Serials, FEFO, Valuation
What it does
docs.text: Stock answers two questions: where is it? and what is it worth? Every movement — a purchase receipt, a delivery, a transfer, a manufacture — writes a Stock Ledger Entry (SLE). The SLE is the memory of stock, the same way the GL Entry is the memory of money. And the same rule applies: never write it by hand.

docs.title: Core DocTypes
docs.text: DocType What it is Item The master: code, name, group, UOM, valuation method, is-stock-item. Warehouse A tree (All Warehouses → Main Store → Cold Room). Stock always sits in one warehouse. Stock Entry Manual movements. Types: Material Issue, Material Receipt, Material Transfer, Manufacture, Repack, Material Transfer for Manufacture. Stock Ledger Entry (SLE) One stock movement line. Created automatically on submit — never insert it by hand. Bin The balance per Item + Warehouse: actual_qty, projected_qty, reserved_qty. Batch A production lot with an expiry date. Enables traceability and FEFO. Serial and Batch Bundle Records exactly which serials / batches a transaction used. Stock Reconciliation The correct way to fix a wrong balance — with a posting date and a reason. Delivery Note Moves stock out (selling side). Purchase Receipt Moves stock in (buying side) and books its value.

docs.title: End-to-end flow
docs.text:
Setup:   Item masters → Warehouses → opening Stock Reconciliation
In:      Purchase Receipt (submit) → SLE in, Bin up, value booked
Move:    Stock Entry — Material Transfer → SLE out of A, SLE in to B
Out:     Delivery Note (submit) → SLE out, Bin down
Make:    Stock Entry — Manufacture → raw materials out, finished goods in
Fix:     Stock Reconciliation (never edit Bin or SLE by hand)
Check:   Stock Balance, Stock Ledger, Stock Ageing reports

Read quantities from Bin or from a stock report — never by summing SLE rows in your own code. And read money from the ledger reports, not from a document's totals after submit.

docs.title: Batches, serials and FEFO
docs.text:
• Batch — one production lot. A batch has a manufacturing date and an expiry date, so a recall can name the exact lot ("recall batch SP-104", not "recall everything").
  • FEFO (First Expiry, First Out) — pick the batch that expires first. Critical for food, pharma and chemicals. ERPNext can auto-select batches by expiry, so the store team does not have to remember.
  • Serials — one unique number per unit (a phone, a machine). The Serial and Batch Bundle records which serials left in which delivery.
  • Valuation — each Item uses FIFO or Moving Average. FIFO values issues at the oldest purchase cost; Moving Average re-computes the average on every receipt. Pick per item and leave it alone — changing it mid-year rewrites history.

docs.title: Worked example — a spice manufacturer, one batch
docs.text:
NexTash's food client (see fmc) receives 500 kg of red chilli as Batch CH-231, expiry 2027-06-30:

  1. Purchase Receipt — 500 kg into "Raw Material Store". Bin: 500 kg.
  2. Production needs 200 kg. The Stock Entry (Manufacture) consumes 200 kg from batch CH-231 and adds 190 kg of chilli powder (10 kg process loss).
  3. A customer order ships 100 kg of powder. The Delivery Note picks the oldest powder batch first — FEFO, so nothing expires on the shelf.
  4. A quality complaint arrives. The batch number on the pack traces back to CH-231, the supplier, the receipt date and every other pack from that lot.

docs.title: A real use case
docs.text:
A pharma distributor was losing stock to expiry: the store picked whatever was nearest, and the oldest batches expired at the back of the shelf. With batches and FEFO picking, the oldest-expiring stock ships first, and the Stock Ageing report shows what will expire in the next 90 days — before it becomes a write-off.

How we can use it: offer batch + FEFO + Stock Ageing as a package to every food and pharma client. It is the same pattern as fmc's batch traceability — and the demo (receive, produce, ship, trace back) closes the sale in one meeting.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Editing Bin or SLE by hand. Wrong balance? Stock Reconciliation with a reason. Hand-edited bins and the ledger disagree forever.
  • No batches for expirable goods. Without batches there is no FEFO and no recall. If it expires, it needs a batch.
  • Summing SLE rows in code to get stock. Use Bin or the Stock Balance report. Summing rows is slow and wrong the moment a backdated entry lands.
  • Changing the valuation method mid-year. FIFO vs Moving Average is a policy decision, not a setting to try. Decide at setup.
  • One warehouse for everything. Separate raw, finished, quarantine and returns warehouses — or "where is it?" has no answer.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: 03 — Selling — from quotation to cash.

docs.title: Selling — Quotations, Sales Orders, Delivery, Pricing
What it does
docs.text: Selling turns a customer's interest into money in the bank — and into stock leaving the warehouse at the right time. Every step is a document, and every document has one job. A Delivery Note moves stock; a Sales Invoice books the sale. Mixing those two jobs up is where selling implementations go wrong.

docs.title: Core DocTypes
docs.text: DocType What it is Customer The master: name, group, territory, default price list, credit limit. Quotation A priced offer. No stock moves, no money booked. Sales Order The confirmed order. Reserves stock, promises a delivery date. Delivery Note Ships the goods. On submit, stock moves out (SLE) and the order becomes "To Bill". Sales Invoice Books the sale. On submit, revenue + tax post to the ledger and the customer owes the money. Payment Entry Records the money received against the invoice. Price List / Item Price What an item costs for a customer group (Retail, Wholesale, Export). Pricing Rule Automatic discounts: "10% off for orders over Rs 100,000". Sales Taxes and Charges Template The tax applied to the invoice.

docs.title: End-to-end flow
docs.text:
Quotation → Sales Order → Delivery Note → Sales Invoice → Payment Entry
   (offer)     (promise)      (ship)          (bill)         (collect)
  • A Quotation can become a Sales Order in one click. The prices carry over.
  • A Delivery Note moves stock out; a Sales Invoice books the sale.
  • An invoice can be created from the order without a delivery — for service sales, where nothing physical ships.
  • Returns use a Sales Invoice with is_return = 1 against the original invoice. Never a negative manual entry.
  • A Sales Order can be partially delivered and partially billed. The status bar tells you what is left: "To Deliver", "To Bill", "Completed".

docs.title: Worked example — a distributor, one order
docs.text:
A retailer orders 200 cartons of cooking oil from Al-Noor Traders:

  1. Quotation — Rs 2,500 per carton, valid 7 days. The retailer accepts.
  2. Sales Order — 200 × 2,500 = Rs 500,000. Submit. The order reserves 200 cartons in the warehouse, and the delivery date is promised.
  3. Delivery Note — 200 cartons leave "Main Store". Submit. Stock drops by 200; the order status becomes "To Bill".
  4. Sales Invoice — Rs 500,000 + 18% sales tax. Submit. Ledger: Dr Customer 590,000 — Cr Sales Income 500,000 — Cr Sales Tax Payable 90,000.
  5. Payment Entry — the retailer pays by bank transfer. The invoice is closed; the order is "Completed".

The same flow works for a service company — skip the Delivery Note and invoice straight from the order.

docs.title: A real use case
docs.text:
A packaging supplier took orders on WhatsApp and wrote deliveries in a register. Orders were forgotten, deliveries were doubled, and nobody knew which customer owed what. After moving to Sales Order → Delivery Note → Sales Invoice, the "To Deliver" list became the morning's work list, and the Accounts Receivable report showed exactly who owed what, with ageing.

How we can use it: make the "To Deliver / To Bill" lists the core of every sales demo — a business owner sees their pending work in one screen, and that is what sells the module. Add Pricing Rules for the client's real discount policy (wholesale slabs, seasonal offers) in the first week, not as an afterthought.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Invoicing before delivery (for goods). The customer owes money for stock still in your warehouse. Invoice after the Delivery Note — unless the sale is a service.
  • Editing a submitted order to change the qty. Cancel and amend. An edited submitted order and its stock/ledger postings will disagree.
  • One price list for everyone. Retail, wholesale and export customers pay different prices. Set up Price Lists and Item Prices properly, or every invoice becomes a manual negotiation.
  • No credit limits. A Customer with no credit limit can order indefinitely. Set limits — ERPNext blocks over-limit orders when configured.
  • Delivery Note as an invoice. It moves stock, it does not book money. If the accountant only has the Delivery Note, the sale never happened in the books.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: 04 — Buying — the mirror image: from need to payment.

docs.title: Buying — Purchase Orders, Receipts, Supplier Workflow
What it does
docs.text: Buying turns a need into stock on the shelf and a bill you can pay. It is the mirror image of Selling: Material Request → Purchase Order → Purchase Receipt → Purchase Invoice → Payment Entry. The same discipline applies — one document, one job. A Purchase Receipt moves stock in; a Purchase Invoice books the liability.

docs.title: Core DocTypes
docs.text: DocType What it is Supplier The master: name, group, default currency, payment terms, tax details. Material Request "We need this." Can be raised by any department; type Purchase, Transfer or Manufacture. Request for Quotation Ask several suppliers for a price on the same items. Supplier Quotation One supplier's priced reply. Purchase Order The confirmed order to one supplier: items, qty, rate, delivery date. Purchase Receipt Goods arrive. On submit, stock moves in and the stock value is booked. Purchase Invoice The supplier's bill. On submit, the liability is booked. Payment Entry Records the money paid against the invoice. Purchase Taxes and Charges Template The tax applied to the purchase invoice.

docs.title: End-to-end flow
docs.text:
Material Request → Purchase Order → Purchase Receipt → Purchase Invoice → Payment Entry
   (we need it)     (we order it)     (it arrived)      (we owe for it)   (we pay)
  • A Purchase Receipt moves stock in and books the stock value. A Purchase Invoice books the supplier liability. They are separate documents.
  • The invoice can arrive before or after the receipt — a supplier may bill first, or deliver first. ERPNext matches them by item and qty, not by date.
  • Returns use a Purchase Invoice with is_return = 1 against the original invoice.
  • The three-way match is the control: Purchase Order (what we ordered) vs Purchase Receipt (what arrived) vs Purchase Invoice (what we are billed). If the three disagree, something is wrong — find it before paying.

docs.title: Worked example — a manufacturer buys raw material
docs.text:
A spice factory needs 500 kg of red chilli:

  1. Material Request — production raises it: 500 kg red chilli, required by Friday.
  2. Request for Quotation — sent to three suppliers. Two reply.
  3. Purchase Order — to the cheaper supplier: 500 kg at Rs 800/kg, delivery Friday. Submit.
  4. Purchase Receipt — Friday, 500 kg arrive and are weighed: 495 kg accepted, 5 kg rejected (damaged). Submit for 495 kg. Stock goes up by 495 kg; the rejected 5 kg never enter stock.
  5. Purchase Invoice — the supplier bills for 500 kg. The invoice is matched against the receipt: only 495 kg are accepted, so the payable is for 495 kg. The 5 kg difference is caught before payment.
  6. Payment Entry — paid on the agreed terms (30 days). Ledger: Dr Supplier — Cr Bank.

docs.title: A real use case
docs.text:
A food manufacturer paid suppliers from the invoice alone, without matching receipts. Short deliveries were paid in full for months. After the three-way match, the Accounts Payable report showed the exact outstanding per supplier, and one supplier's repeated short-shipments were visible in the Purchase Receipt history — the evidence for a renegotiation.

How we can use it: demo the three-way match (order vs receipt vs invoice) in every buying pitch — it is the one screen that makes a finance head trust the system. For manufacturing clients, start the flow at Material Request from production, not at the Purchase Order, so the need is visible before the money is committed.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Paying from the invoice without the receipt. If the goods never arrived, you just paid for air. Always match receipt first.
  • One supplier, one price, forever. No Supplier Quotation comparison means no leverage. Get two quotes on anything recurring.
  • Booking the invoice for the ordered qty, not the received qty. The payable must match what arrived. Short-shipments are the classic leak.
  • No Material Request. Orders raised directly by purchasing hide the real need. The request is the audit trail — who asked, for what, and why.
  • Editing a submitted receipt to fix a qty. Cancel and amend. A receipt posts stock; editing it leaves the stock ledger wrong.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: You have finished the Core modules: Accounting, Stock, Selling, Buying. Next in the ERPNext path: Operations — Manufacturing, Quality, Projects and Assets (Beta).

docs.title: Manufacturing — BOM, Work Orders, Job Cards, Production, Subcontracting
What it does
docs.text:
Manufacturing turns raw material into finished goods — and proves the cost of every unit that comes out. The recipe is the BOM (Bill of Materials), the order to make something is the Work Order, and the work done on the shop floor is tracked on Job Cards. When the Work Order finishes, a Stock Entry moves raw materials out and finished goods in, and the ledger books the production cost.

If you skip Manufacturing and just do Stock Entries, you lose the two things a factory owner cares about: what it cost and where it got stuck.

docs.title: Core DocTypes
docs.text: DocType What it is BOM The recipe: finished item + raw materials + operations + cost. One BOM per item (with variants by version). BOM Creator A faster way to build a multi-level BOM from a finished item downwards. Work Order "Make 500 kg of this." Carries the BOM, qty, warehouse, planned dates, and status. Job Card One operation on the shop floor (grinding, packing). Tracks time, operator, and completed qty. Routing The ordered list of operations a product goes through. Operation One step: name, workstation, standard time. Workstation A machine or work centre (grinder, packing line) with an hourly rate. Production Plan The planner: turns Sales Orders / forecasts into Work Orders and Material Requests. Master Production Schedule The plan for what to make, by period, before the Production Plan runs. Sales Forecast Expected demand per item, per period — the input to the schedule. Stock Entry (Manufacture) The movement: raw materials out, finished goods in. Posted when the Work Order completes. Downtime Entry Records when a workstation stopped, and why. Subcontracting Order Send raw material to an outside vendor to do one step (e.g. packing). Subcontracting Receipt The finished work comes back from the vendor. Subcontracting Inward Order The reverse (v16): a customer sends you material and you do the work.

docs.title: End-to-end flow
docs.text:
Setup:   Item masters → BOM → Routing + Workstations → Operations
Plan:    Sales Forecast → Master Production Schedule → Production Plan
Order:   Work Order (submit) → materials reserved / transferred to WIP
Make:    Job Card per operation → time logged → Stock Entry (Manufacture)
Cost:    finished goods valued at BOM cost + labour + overhead
Check:   Work Order Summary, Production Plan, Job Card, BOM Cost reports
  • A Work Order starts from a BOM. Change the BOM and every future Work Order changes with it — that is why the BOM, not the Work Order, is the master.
  • Materials move to the work-in-progress warehouse with a Stock Entry of type Material Transfer for Manufacture; the finished goods come back with Manufacture.
  • A Job Card is the shop-floor truth: who did it, how long it took, how much was made. Without Job Cards you cannot cost labour or find the slow operation.
  • Subcontracting is for the step you do not do yourself: the Subcontracting Order sends the material out, the Subcontracting Receipt brings the finished work back, and the vendor is paid for the service.

docs.title: Worked example — a spice manufacturer, one Work Order
docs.text:
The fmc demo client (fmc — Food Manufacturing for ERPNext) needs 500 kg of red chilli powder:

  1. BOM for "Chilli Powder 500g pack": 1 kg raw chilli, 0.02 kg packaging, operations: cleaning → grinding → packing.
  2. Work Order for 500 kg. Submit. 500 kg of raw chilli (Batch CH-231) moves to the WIP warehouse.
  3. Job Cards: cleaning (2 hrs), grinding (4 hrs on the grinder workstation), packing (3 hrs). Each card logs time and operator.
  4. Stock Entry (Manufacture): 500 kg raw chilli consumed, 490 kg powder produced (10 kg process loss), packed into 980 packs of 500 g.
  5. The packs carry the production batch, so a customer complaint traces back to CH-231, the grinder, the operator and the day it was made.

docs.title: A real use case
docs.text:
A Lahore spice factory planned production in a notebook and costed it by feel. They never knew which product actually made money — grinding losses and packing time were invisible. After BOMs + Work Orders + Job Cards, the BOM cost report showed the real cost per pack, and the slow operation (grinding) was visible on the Job Card report — the case for a second grinder, with numbers.

How we can use it: sell Manufacturing to every food, pharma and textile client as the module that answers "what does it cost?" — and demo it with fmc, which already has the food-manufacturing flow (batches, FEFO, QC) built in. Subcontracting is a separate fixed-price add-on for clients who outsource packing or stitching.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• No BOM, just Stock Entries. Production without a BOM has no standard cost and no variance — you cannot tell if a batch was efficient or wasteful.
  • Skipping Job Cards. Without them, labour cost is a guess and the bottleneck operation stays hidden.
  • One warehouse for raw, WIP and finished. Materials get mixed up and "where is it?" has no answer. Separate them.
  • Editing a submitted Work Order to change the qty. Cancel and amend — the Work Order has already reserved and moved stock.
  • Forgetting subcontracting receipts. Material sent out and never received back is stock that quietly disappears from the books.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: 06 — Quality — inspections, quarantine, release and reject.

docs.title: Quality — Inspections, QC Quarantine / Release / Hold / Reject
What it does
docs.text: Quality decides whether goods are good enough to use, sell or ship — and keeps the bad ones out of stock. A Quality Inspection checks a receipt, a production batch or a delivery against a Quality Inspection Template (a list of parameters with acceptance values). Goods that fail go to a quarantine warehouse, not back into sellable stock. Quality Goals, Procedures and Reviews are the management side: the targets, the written process, and the regular check that the process is working.

docs.title: Core DocTypes
docs.text:
DocType What it is Quality Inspection One inspection: what was checked, against which template, pass or fail. Quality Inspection Template The checklist: parameters, acceptance values, per item or item group. Quality Inspection Parameter One measurable check (moisture %, colour, weight) with a value or range. Quality Inspection Reading One measured value recorded during an inspection. Quality Goal A measurable target (e.g. "rejection rate under 2%") with an owner. Quality Procedure The written process for a quality activity. Quality Action A corrective or preventive action raised from a failure. Quality Review A periodic review of goals, actions and inspection results. Quality Feedback Feedback from a customer or internal team about quality. Quality Meeting The meeting record: agenda, minutes, actions.

Inspections live in the Stock module (they attach to receipts, deliveries and production), while goals, procedures and reviews are the quality management system around them.

docs.title: End-to-end flow
docs.text:
Setup:   Quality Inspection Templates per item → quarantine warehouse
In:      Purchase Receipt → Quality Inspection → Accepted / Rejected
Fail:    rejected qty → quarantine warehouse (never into sellable stock)
Fix:     Quality Action (return to supplier, rework, or scrap)
Make:    in-process inspection on the Work Order → out-going inspection
Check:   Quality Inspection report, rejection rate vs Quality Goal
  • An inspection is linked to a reference document — usually a Purchase Receipt, a Delivery Note or a Stock Entry. The inspected qty is accepted or rejected on that document.
  • Accepted stock goes to the normal warehouse. Rejected stock goes to the quarantine warehouse (or is returned). It is never silently added to sellable stock.
  • A Quality Goal turns inspection results into a number the owner watches — rejection rate, on-time inspections, complaints per month.
  • A Quality Action is what happens after a failure: return the lot, rework it, change the supplier, or change the process. Without the action, the same failure repeats next month.

docs.title: Worked example — a spice manufacturer, one rejected lot
docs.text:
The fmc demo client (fmc) receives 500 kg of red chilli:

  1. Purchase Receipt — 500 kg arrive. The item has a Quality Inspection Template (moisture ≤ 10%, colour grade A, no stones).
  2. Quality Inspection — the lab measures moisture 13%. The lot fails.
  3. 500 kg go to the quarantine warehouse. The 5 kg sample is kept for the supplier dispute; the rest is not usable.
  4. Quality Action — return to supplier, and add a pre-shipment moisture check to the supplier's terms. The rejected lot never reaches production, so no finished batch is contaminated.
  5. The Quality Goal "rejection rate under 2%" shows this supplier at 8% over the quarter — the evidence for switching suppliers.

docs.title: A real use case
docs.text:
A food exporter shipped a container that a buyer rejected on arrival for moisture — the whole shipment was lost. The receipt had never been inspected because "the supplier is trusted". After incoming inspections with a quarantine warehouse, bad lots are caught at the gate, and the rejection report shows which suppliers cost money — before the container sails.

How we can use it: bundle Quality with every Manufacturing and Buying implementation for food and pharma clients — incoming inspection on Purchase Receipt is a one-day setup that prevents the most expensive failure a client can have (a rejected shipment). The Quality Goal dashboard is the phase-2 sale.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• No quarantine warehouse. Rejected stock mixed into sellable stock is a recall waiting to happen.
  • Inspecting after use. An inspection on the Delivery Note is too late — inspect at receipt, before the material enters production.
  • A template with no numbers. "Looks fine" is not a parameter. Every check needs an acceptance value (moisture ≤ 10%, not "dry enough").
  • Failures with no Quality Action. The same lot fails next month from the same supplier. Log the action, assign an owner, close it.
  • Skipping in-process inspection. Catching a problem at the finished pack stage wastes the whole batch — check during production.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: 07 — Projects — tasks, timesheets, costing.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text: Projects turns "do this work for a client" into something measurable: a Project with Tasks, time booked on Timesheets, costs collected from timesheets, expenses and purchases — and a profit number at the end. Without it, a services business knows its revenue and guesses its cost. With it, every project shows whether it made money or lost it, while there is still time to fix it.

docs.title: Core DocTypes
docs.text: DocType What it is Project The job: client, dates, expected dates, costing, billing status. Task One piece of work in a project, with an owner, dates and dependencies. Timesheet Time booked against a project / task, with billable and costing rates. Timesheet Detail One time entry: hours, activity type, billable or not. Activity Type The kind of work (Development, Consulting, Support) with a costing and billing rate. Activity Cost The cost rate for an Activity Type per employee. Project Template A reusable task list for a standard job (e.g. "ERPNext go-live"). Project Type A category (Internal, External, Support) for grouping and reporting. Project Update A status note on the project, shared with the team.

docs.title: End-to-end flow
docs.text:
Setup:   Activity Types + rates → Project Template for the standard job
Plan:    Project → Tasks (with dependencies) → assign owners
Work:    Timesheet entries against tasks (billable / non-billable)
Cost:    timesheets + Expense Claims + Purchase Invoices roll into the project
Bill:    Timesheet → Sales Invoice (time billed to the client)
Check:   Project Profitability report — revenue vs cost, per project
  • A Task can depend on another Task — it cannot start until the first is done. Dependencies are what make the plan honest.
  • A Timesheet entry has two rates: the costing rate (what the hour costs you) and the billing rate (what you charge). Profit is the gap between them.
  • Billable hours go to the client invoice; non-billable hours are still cost — they just do not earn. Marking everything billable hides the real margin.
  • The Project Profitability report is the one number the owner checks: revenue booked minus cost incurred, per project.

docs.title: Worked example — an ERPNext implementation, one project
docs.text:
NexTash takes an ERPNext implementation for a Lahore distributor:

  1. Project "Al-Noor ERPNext Go-Live", type External, from the "ERPNext go-live" Project Template: setup → data import → training → go-live, with dependencies in order.
  2. Tasks assigned: Irfaan (setup, data import), a colleague (training).
  3. Each week the team books Timesheets: 30 hrs Development (billable), 6 hrs internal meetings (non-billable).
  4. Travel and a test server land as Expense Claims and a Purchase Invoice against the project.
  5. At month end, the Sales Invoice bills the 30 hours at the agreed rate. The Project Profitability report shows revenue 450,000, cost 280,000 — the project is on track, and the 6 non-billable hours are visible, not hidden.

docs.title: A real use case
docs.text:
A services company billed clients from memory at month end — hours were forgotten, and nobody knew which client was profitable. After Projects + Timesheets, every invoice came from booked time, and the profitability report showed one "big" client was actually loss-making once internal hours were counted. They repriced that client with the report as evidence.

How we can use it: run NexTash's own client work in Projects — it is both our internal tool and the demo. When a client asks "how do you track our project?", show them the live project: tasks, timesheets, profitability. That demo sells the module better than any slide.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Timesheets filled at month end. Memory is not a time record. Book time daily, or the billable hours are a guess.
  • No costing rate. If only the billing rate is set, the project looks profitable until salaries are counted.
  • Everything marked billable. Internal work billed to a client is a dispute waiting to happen — and it hides the real cost.
  • Tasks with no owner and no dates. A task list without owners is a wish list. Every task needs one owner and one due date.
  • Ignoring the profitability report. The report exists to catch a losing project early. Check it weekly, not at the end.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: 08 — Assets — asset lifecycle, depreciation, maintenance.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text: Assets tracks the things a business owns that last more than a year — machines, vehicles, computers, furniture — from purchase to disposal. An Asset is created from a Purchase Invoice, depreciated on a schedule so the books show its falling value, maintained on a plan so it does not break, moved between locations so it is not lost, and scrapped or sold at the end. Without it, a business owns things it cannot find and depreciates things it no longer has.

docs.title: Core DocTypes
docs.text: DocType What it is Asset One owned item: value, location, custodian, status, depreciation schedule. Asset Category The group (Plant & Machinery, Vehicles, IT Equipment) with its accounts and depreciation defaults. Asset Depreciation Schedule The depreciation plan per finance book: method, rate, dates, amounts. Asset Maintenance The maintenance plan for an asset: tasks and their frequency. Asset Maintenance Task One recurring task (oil change every 3 months) in a maintenance plan. Asset Maintenance Log One completed maintenance event, with cost. Asset Movement Moving an asset between locations or custodians. Asset Repair A repair job: what broke, what it cost, when it was fixed. Asset Value Adjustment Revalue an asset up or down (revaluation or impairment). Asset Capitalization Capitalize stock items or services into an asset (e.g. building a machine from parts). Location Where assets live: a tree (Factory → Hall A → Line 1).

docs.title: End-to-end flow
docs.text:
Setup:   Asset Categories (accounts + method) → Locations
Buy:     Purchase Invoice → Asset created (or capitalised from stock)
Value:   Asset Depreciation Schedule runs → depreciation posts to the ledger
Use:     Asset Movement when it changes location or custodian
Care:    Asset Maintenance plan → Asset Maintenance Log per visit
Fix:     Asset Repair when it breaks
End:     sell or scrap → Asset Value Adjustment / disposal, ledger updated
Check:   Fixed Asset Register, Asset Depreciation report
  • Depreciation methods: Straight Line (same amount every period), Written Down Value (a % of the remaining value), Double Declining Balance, or Manual. Pick per category, not per asset, and do not change it mid-life.
  • The Fixed Asset Register is the audit answer to "what do we own?": every asset, its location, its custodian, its book value.
  • Asset Movement is the control that stops assets walking away — a machine moved without a Movement entry is a machine the register cannot find.

docs.title: Worked example — a factory, one machine
docs.text:
A spice factory buys a grinder for Rs 1,200,000:

  1. Purchase Invoice — the grinder is booked. An Asset is created from it, category "Plant & Machinery", location "Factory → Hall A", custodian the production supervisor.
  2. Asset Depreciation Schedule — Straight Line, 10% per year, 10 years. Each month Rs 10,000 depreciation posts to the ledger automatically.
  3. Asset Maintenance — oil change every 3 months, belt check every 6. Each visit is logged in an Asset Maintenance Log with its cost.
  4. Year 3, the motor burns out. Asset Repair — Rs 85,000, two days downtime. The repair cost is visible against the asset, not hidden in general expenses.
  5. Year 8, the grinder is sold for Rs 300,000. Book value is Rs 240,000 — the Rs 60,000 gain is booked on disposal, and the asset leaves the register.

docs.title: A real use case
docs.text:
A manufacturer had 40 machines across two halls and no register. When the auditor asked for the fixed asset list, the accountant guessed from old invoices — including machines sold years ago. After Assets, the Fixed Asset Register matched the floor, depreciation posted monthly without manual journals, and the maintenance log showed which machine cost the most in repairs — the case for replacing it.

How we can use it: offer the Fixed Asset Register as the audit-ready deliverable in every manufacturing implementation — auditors ask for it by name, and a client who has it will not go back. Maintenance plans are the phase-2 sale to any client with plant and machinery.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assets booked as expenses. A Rs 1,200,000 machine in "General Expense" breaks the balance sheet and the tax return. Capitalise it.
  • Depreciation as manual journals. Monthly manual journals drift and get forgotten. Use the schedule — it posts itself.
  • No Location or custodian. An asset with no location is an asset that cannot be found. Set both at creation.
  • Repairs hidden in expenses. If repair cost is not on the asset, you cannot see which machine is eating money.
  • Changing the depreciation method mid-life. It rewrites the book value history. Decide at setup, per category.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: 09 — HR — employees, leave, payroll, attendance.

docs.title: HR — Employees, Leave, Attendance, Payroll, Shifts
What it does
docs.text: HR runs the people side of the business: who works here, when they are off, whether they showed up, and what they are paid. An Employee gets leave allocated, applies for it, is marked present or absent, works a Shift, and is paid through a Salary Slip generated by a Payroll Entry. In v16 the HR module is the separate Frappe HR app (hrms) — the Employee master itself still sits in ERPNext core, and HRMS builds on it.

docs.title: Core DocTypes
docs.text: DocType What it is Employee The master: name, company, department, designation, date of joining, reports-to. Leave Type A kind of leave: Annual, Sick, Casual — with its rules. Leave Allocation Grants leave days to an employee for a period. Leave Application The request: dates, leave type, approver. Posts to the leave ledger on submit. Leave Ledger Entry One leave movement. Created automatically — never insert it by hand. Attendance One day's record: Present, Absent, Half Day, On Leave. Employee Checkin One punch: in or out, with time (from biometric or manual entry). Shift Type A shift: start, end, late-entry and early-exit rules. Shift Assignment Puts an employee on a shift for a period. Holiday List The year's holidays, per company or location. Salary Structure The pay design: earnings and deductions (basic, allowances, tax, provident fund). Salary Structure Assignment Assigns a structure to an employee from a date. Salary Slip One month's pay for one employee: gross, deductions, net. Payroll Entry The payroll run: generates Salary Slips for a set of employees. Expense Claim An employee's claim (travel, fuel) for approval and payment.

docs.title: End-to-end flow
docs.text:
Setup:   Departments → Holiday List → Leave Types → Shift Types → Salary Structures
Hire:    Employee → Leave Allocation → Shift Assignment → Salary Structure Assignment
Daily:   Employee Checkin → Attendance (auto-marked from checkins)
Leave:   Leave Application (submit) → balance drops → Attendance shows On Leave
Pay:     Payroll Entry → Salary Slips → Payment Entry (bank) → ledger
Check:   Leave Balance, Attendance, Salary Register reports
  • Leave Allocation grants the days; Leave Application spends them. No allocation, no application — the balance goes negative and the report shows it.
  • Attendance can be marked from Employee Checkin (biometric or manual punches) or entered directly. Checkins are the audit trail; attendance is the record payroll reads.
  • Payroll Entry is the run: pick the period and the employees, and it generates the Salary Slips. A slip is per employee per month — never edit a submitted slip, cancel and regenerate it.
  • Salary Structure is where the pay policy lives: basic pay, house rent, medical, tax and provident fund as components. Change the policy in the structure, not in individual slips.

docs.title: Worked example — a factory, one month
docs.text:
A spice factory has 45 staff on two shifts:

  1. Employees created with department, designation and joining date. Holiday List for the year, Shift Types Morning (8–4) and Evening (4–12), Shift Assignments per worker.
  2. Daily, workers punch in. Employee Checkin records feed Attendance — Present, Late, or Absent.
  3. A worker applies for 3 days annual leave. Leave Application approved; balance drops from 12 to 9; those days show On Leave.
  4. Month end: Payroll Entry generates 45 Salary Slips. Late days deduct per the salary structure; leave days are paid. Slips are submitted and paid by bank in one Payment Entry.
  5. The Salary Register shows gross, deductions and net per employee — the same report the accountant files with.

docs.title: A real use case
docs.text:
A 60-person company ran attendance in a register and payroll in Excel. Leave balances lived in the HR head's memory, and salary day took three days of rechecking. After HR, checkins mark attendance automatically, leave balances are visible to everyone, and the payroll run takes an afternoon — with the Salary Register as the audit record.

How we can use it: sell HR as the second module after Accounting for any client with 20+ staff — attendance + leave + payroll is the package every growing business feels the pain of. Biometric checkin sync is a small fixed-price add-on (see the apps catalog's HR entries).

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Leave without allocation. Applications against zero balance create negative balances and arguments at year end.
  • Payroll from edited slips. A submitted Salary Slip is a record — cancel and regenerate, never edit.
  • No Shift Assignment. Without it, checkins have nothing to compare against and "late" has no meaning.
  • Salary policy in slips, not structures. The same allowance typed into 45 slips is 45 chances to be wrong. Put it in the structure.
  • Attendance marked by hand daily. Use checkins. Manual attendance for 45 people is a full-time job and a source of disputes.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: 10 — CRM — leads, deals, web forms (Frappe CRM).

docs.title: CRM — Leads, Deals, Web Forms (Frappe CRM)
What it does
docs.text: CRM turns strangers into customers: capture a Lead, qualify it, work it as a Deal through stages, and close it. Use Frappe CRM — the separate app — not the legacy CRM inside ERPNext. The legacy module (Lead, Opportunity in ERPNext core) is scheduled for deprecation and will be completely removed in version 17, and Frappe CRM is where all new development happens: web forms for lead capture, deal pipelines, enrichment, and workflow automations. In November 2026 it was renumbered to the Framework scheme (v16.x targets Frappe v16) and runs on ~2,500 paid sites.

docs.title: Core DocTypes
docs.text:
DocType What it is CRM Lead One prospect: name, contact, source, status. The top of the funnel. CRM Deal One opportunity: value, stage, probability, expected close date. CRM Organization The company a lead or deal belongs to. CRM Task A follow-up: call, visit, send a quote — with a due date and owner. CRM Call Log One call: who, when, what was said, next step. FCRM Note A note on a lead or deal. CRM Lead Status / CRM Deal Status The pipeline stages (New, Contacted, Qualified, Won, Lost). CRM Service Level Agreement Response-time targets for leads (first reply within X hours). CRM Form Script Scripting for the CRM's web forms (validation, defaults).

Install it with bench get-app crm — it is a separate app, not part of ERPNext core. Leads captured on the website arrive through the CRM's web forms; a lead becomes a deal when it is qualified, and a deal becomes a Customer + Quotation in ERPNext when it is won.

docs.title: End-to-end flow
docs.text:
Capture:  web form / email / manual → CRM Lead
Qualify:  Lead → contact, understand the need → convert to CRM Deal
Work:     CRM Deal through stages → CRM Task + CRM Call Log per step
Close:    Won → Customer + Quotation in ERPNext → Sales Order
Lose:     Lost → CRM Lost Reason recorded (the data that fixes the funnel)
Check:   CRM dashboard — pipeline value, conversion rate, ageing deals
  • A Lead is unqualified interest; a Deal is a qualified opportunity with a value. Converting too early fills the pipeline with noise; converting too late means nobody follows up.
  • Every deal needs a next step — a CRM Task with a date and an owner. A deal with no next step is a deal that dies quietly.
  • Lost Reason is the most valuable field in the CRM. "Too expensive" ten times in a row is a pricing problem, not a sales problem.
  • The CRM has its own Service Level Agreement: first response within a set time. Leads answered late are leads lost to a competitor.

docs.title: Worked example — NexTash, one lead to one project
docs.text:
A food manufacturer fills the "Get a quote" form on the NexTash site:

  1. CRM Lead created automatically from the web form: company, contact, "ERPNext for spice factory", source Website.
  2. Irfaan calls the same day. CRM Call Log: "wants Manufacturing + Quality, 40 users, currently on Excel". Lead status → Qualified.
  3. CRM Deal created: value Rs 1,800,000, stage "Proposal", close date next month. CRM Tasks: send proposal (Tue), follow-up call (Fri).
  4. The client accepts. Deal → Won. A Customer and Quotation are created in ERPNext, and the work starts as a Project (see lesson 07).
  5. The dashboard shows the funnel: 12 leads this month, 5 qualified, 2 won — and the lost deals say "no budget this quarter", which is a follow-up list for next quarter, not a dead end.

docs.title: A real use case
docs.text:
A distributor's sales team kept leads in personal WhatsApp chats. When a salesperson left, the leads left with him. After Frappe CRM, every lead is in the system with an owner and a next step, the manager sees the whole pipeline in one dashboard, and a lead unanswered for 24 hours is visible — not discovered a month later.

How we can use it: use Frappe CRM for NexTash's own pipeline first — it is the demo every sales call starts from. Then sell it to every client whose sales run on WhatsApp and memory: unlimited agents, no per-seat fee, and the web form turns their website into a lead machine. Always install Frappe CRM on new projects; never start a client on the legacy ERPNext CRM.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Using the legacy ERPNext CRM. It is scheduled for removal in v17. New implementations go on Frappe CRM, full stop.
  • Leads with no owner and no next step. An unowned lead is a lost lead. Every lead needs an owner the day it arrives.
  • No Lost Reason. A lost deal without a reason teaches nothing. Record it every time.
  • Deals stuck at one stage for weeks. An ageing deal is a dead deal with the stage left open. Review the pipeline weekly and close or re-date.
  • No web form. If leads only arrive by phone, the website is doing nothing. The form is a one-hour setup.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: 11 — Helpdesk — tickets, SLAs, support workflow.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text: Helpdesk turns support chaos into a queue: every request becomes an HD Ticket with a type, a priority, an owner, and a clock. The clock is the Service Level Agreement — first response and resolution targets that the team is measured against. Tickets arrive from email, the customer portal or a form; agents work them in a team; and the knowledge base (HD Article) answers the question before it becomes a ticket. Frappe Helpdesk is a separate app (bench get-app helpdesk), renumbered to v16.x in November 2026 — unlimited agents, no per-seat fee.

docs.title: Core DocTypes
docs.text: DocType What it is HD Ticket One request: customer, subject, type, priority, status, agent, SLA. HD Agent A support agent: who can be assigned tickets. HD Team A group of agents (e.g. "ERP Support", "Billing"). HD Service Level Agreement Response and resolution targets per priority and customer. HD Service Level Priority One priority's targets inside an SLA (e.g. Urgent: 1 hr response). HD Ticket Type The kind of request: Bug, Question, Feature Request. HD Ticket Priority Urgent, High, Medium, Low. HD Ticket Status Open, Replied, Resolved, Closed. HD Customer A customer in Helpdesk, linked to their ERPNext Customer. HD Article One knowledge-base article, in a category. HD Article Category A section of the knowledge base (Getting Started, Billing). HD Saved Reply A canned response for a common answer. HD Ticket Template A form template for raising a ticket (fields per type).

docs.title: End-to-end flow
docs.text:
Raise:    email / portal / form → HD Ticket (auto-created, type + priority set)
Assign:   ticket → HD Team → HD Agent (round-robin or manual)
Work:     agent replies, ticket moves Open → Replied → Resolved
Clock:    SLA measures first response and resolution against targets
Close:    customer confirms → Closed; feedback requested
Learn:    repeated questions → HD Article → fewer tickets next month
Check:   ticket ageing, SLA breach, first-response time reports
  • A ticket has one owner at a time. An unassigned ticket is a ticket nobody is working on — the queue view makes that visible.
  • The SLA clock starts when the ticket is created and pauses when the agent waits for the customer. Breaches are the report the support lead checks every morning.
  • HD Article is the cheapest support there is: every question answered once in the knowledge base is a ticket that never arrives.
  • A Saved Reply keeps answers consistent — the same question gets the same correct answer, whoever is on shift.

docs.title: Worked example — NexTash support, one week
docs.text:
A client's user cannot post a Purchase Receipt:

  1. She emails support. An HD Ticket is auto-created: type Question, priority High, customer linked to their ERPNext Customer.
  2. The ticket lands in the "ERP Support" team queue and is assigned to an agent. The SLA says first response within 4 hours.
  3. The agent finds the cause — a missing permission on the Purchase Receipt DocType — and replies with the fix. Status → Replied.
  4. The client confirms it works. Status → Resolved → Closed.
  5. The same question arrives from a second client. The agent writes an HD Article ("Why you cannot submit a Purchase Receipt") and a Saved Reply pointing to it. The third time, the answer takes 30 seconds.

docs.title: A real use case
docs.text:
A software company ran support from a shared inbox. The same question was answered five different ways, urgent requests sat behind routine ones, and nobody knew how many tickets were open. After Helpdesk, the queue showed the real workload, the SLA report showed first-response time dropping from a day to two hours, and the knowledge base cut repeat tickets by a third.

How we can use it: run NexTash's own client support on Helpdesk — it is the demo and the tool in one. Then sell it to any client whose support runs on a shared inbox or WhatsApp: the SLA report is the pitch ("your customers will know you answer in hours, not days"), and the knowledge base is the phase-2 sale.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• No SLA. Without targets, "urgent" is an opinion and response time is whatever happened. Set the SLA on day one.
  • Tickets with no owner. The queue must show unassigned tickets prominently — or they rot.
  • Resolving without confirming. A ticket closed before the customer confirms is a ticket that reopens angrier.
  • No knowledge base. Answering the same question ten times is ten tickets that an article would have prevented.
  • Support in a shared inbox. Email has no queue, no owner, no clock. That is exactly what Helpdesk replaces.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: 12 — Support & Portal — customer portal, communication, portal users.

docs.title: Support & Portal — Customer Portal, Communication, Portal Users
What it does
docs.text: The portal is where customers help themselves: they log in and see their orders, invoices, payments and support tickets — without emailing anyone. A Portal User is a contact given a login linked to a Customer; the portal shows them only their own documents. Behind it is communication: every email, call and comment on a document is recorded on that document, so the full history of a customer is one click away. The portal turns "where is my order?" from a support ticket into a page the customer opens themselves.

docs.title: Core DocTypes
docs.text: DocType What it is Portal User A login for a customer contact: user, Customer, roles. The child table on Customer that grants portal access. Customer The master: the portal shows this customer's own orders, invoices and tickets. Contact The person at the customer: email, phone — becomes a Portal User when given access. HD Customer The Helpdesk side of a customer: links their tickets to the ERPNext Customer. HD Ticket What the customer raises and tracks in the portal. Web Form A public form (lead capture, ticket raising, feedback) that writes into the system. Website Settings The site configuration behind the portal pages. Issue The legacy ERPNext support ticket (being replaced by HD Ticket). Email / Comment Communication recorded on a document — the history of every conversation.

docs.title: End-to-end flow
docs.text:
Setup:   Customer → Contact → Portal User (login + roles)
Visit:   customer logs in → sees their Sales Orders, Invoices, Payments
Ask:     customer raises an HD Ticket from the portal
Track:   ticket status visible in the portal; replies by email + portal
Pay:     customer sees outstanding invoices and pays (where configured)
Check:   portal usage, open tickets per customer, ageing receivables
  • A Portal User sees only their own Customer's documents — User Permissions enforce it. A portal login that can see another customer's invoices is a data leak; test it with a real portal account before go-live.
  • Every email and comment is stored on the document it belongs to. When a customer calls, the history is on their Sales Order or ticket — nobody has to search an inbox.
  • A Web Form is the public front door: a lead form, a ticket form, a feedback form. It writes straight into the system, so nothing is re-typed.
  • For a richer portal (custom pages, dashboards, document libraries), build it with Frappe Builder — the website builder that ships with the Frappe stack.

docs.title: Worked example — a distributor, one customer
docs.text:
Al-Noor Traders supplies 200 retailers. One retailer, "Karachi Mart", keeps calling to ask where its delivery is:

  1. A Contact (the store manager) is created on the Customer and given a Portal User login.
  2. He logs in and sees his Sales Orders (what is promised), Delivery Notes (what shipped, with dates) and Sales Invoices (what is owed).
  3. A delivery is short. He raises an HD Ticket from the portal — it lands in the support queue with his Customer already linked.
  4. The agent replies; the answer and the ticket status are visible in the portal. The next "where is my order?" call never happens.
  5. Month end, the store manager downloads his own statement from the portal — no one at Al-Noor has to send it.

docs.title: A real use case
docs.text:
A supplier's sales team spent an hour a day answering "where is my order?" and emailing statements. After the portal, customers checked orders themselves, statements were self-service, and the support queue shrank — the team spent the hour selling instead. The portal also became the reason one big customer stayed: "your competitors make us call for everything."

How we can use it: include the portal in every B2B implementation as the self-service add-on — it is a small setup (Portal Users + permissions) with a visible payoff the client's customers feel. A Builder-built custom portal page is a fixed-price upsell for clients who want more than the standard pages.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Portal access without testing permissions. Always log in as a real portal user and check they see only their own documents.
  • Portal Users for the wrong contacts. Only people who should see the account get a login — not every email on the account.
  • Communication outside the system. Deals agreed on WhatsApp and never recorded are deals the next person cannot see. Log it on the document.
  • No ticket form in the portal. If customers can only email, the portal is a display window, not a channel. Add the form.
  • Hiding the portal. A portal nobody is told about is a portal nobody uses. Announce it at go-live, with logins sent to every customer.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: 13 — Studio, Flow & Insights — the new v16 tools in Desk.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text: v16.60 (17 Nov 2026) moved three things into the core Desk experience. Studio — the drag-and-drop app builder — merged into Framework, so small apps are built visually, without code. Frappe Flow (beta) is the AI harness inside Desk: an LLM that analyses your data and fills forms, permission-aware, using your own AI keys. Insights dashboards now embed in Desk, so managers see live charts where they work instead of exporting to Excel. Together they change what a "customisation" is: from a developer task to something an analyst can build in a day.

docs.title: Core pieces
docs.text:
Piece What it is Studio Build a mini-app visually: pages, layouts, data sources, CRUD — no code. Apps are standard Frappe apps under the hood. Frappe Flow The AI harness in Desk (beta): ask questions of your data, draft documents, fill forms — the AI only sees what the user may see. Insights Dashboard A live dashboard in Desk: charts and numbers from ERP data, refreshed on open. Insights Workbook A set of related queries and charts, worked on like a spreadsheet of live data. Insights Query One question against the data (SQL or visual builder). Insights Data Source Where a query reads from: a DocType, a table, or an external database. Insights Chart One chart built from a query.

Studio builds apps; Flow talks about your data; Insights shows it. None of them replaces the modules — they sit on top of them.

docs.title: End-to-end flow
docs.text:
Build:   Studio → new mini-app (e.g. gate pass, sample tracking) → publish to Desktop
Ask:     Flow → "which customers are overdue?" → answer from live data, permission-aware
See:     Insights Dashboard → sales, stock, finance charts embedded in Desk
Act:     dashboard number → drill into the document → fix it there
  • Studio is for the small app that does not justify a developer: visitor register, gate pass, sample tracking, asset check-in. Build it visually, publish it to the Desktop, and it behaves like any other app.
  • Flow is permission-aware by design: it can only see what the signed- in user can see. It does not bypass permissions, and it uses your own AI keys — the data goes to your AI provider, not to Frappe.
  • Insights in Desk means the dashboard is where the work happens. Build the query once, put the chart on a dashboard, and the manager opens Desk and sees it — no export, no stale spreadsheet.
  • v16.61 added Flow public agents and an AI assistant that can view images — the harness is being extended every month on the new monthly release train.

docs.title: Worked example — a gate pass app in a day
docs.text:
A factory's gate pass is a paper slip: who took what out, signed by the guard:

  1. In Studio, an analyst builds a "Gate Pass" mini-app: a form (item, qty, vehicle, driver, purpose), a list view, and an approval step.
  2. The app is published to the Desktop. The guard opens it on a phone and logs each pass; the store manager approves from Desk.
  3. The manager asks Flow: "how many gate passes this week, and for which items?" — the answer comes from the live data, with the numbers.
  4. An Insights Dashboard shows passes per day and the top items leaving the gate — the first sign of a pilferage pattern, visible without anyone running a report.

docs.title: A real use case
docs.text:
A client's quality head wanted a sample-tracking register — samples sent to labs, results back, expiry dates. As a coded app it was a two-week job; in Studio it was built in a day by an analyst, with the lab results entering through a form the lab technician could use. The client got the app in the same week they asked for it — and asked for two more.

How we can use it: offer Studio-built mini-apps as a new service line — fixed-price, built in days, billed per app. Train one NexTash analyst on Studio so small apps stop consuming developer time. Offer Flow as a pilot to one friendly client on a test site ("ask your ERP" on their own data) before selling it widely.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Building in Studio what belongs in a module. If the app is really Manufacturing or HR, use the module. Studio is for the gap around the modules, not a replacement for them.
  • Trusting Flow's answer without checking. Flow analyses data; it can misread it. The answer is a starting point — verify against the report.
  • Dashboards nobody opens. A dashboard buried three clicks deep is decoration. Put the one number that matters on the Desktop.
  • Giving the AI keys nobody owns. Flow uses your own AI keys — decide whose account and budget they are before the pilot, not after the bill.
  • Skipping the permission check. Flow respects permissions, but the underlying roles must be right first — an over-permissioned user makes the AI over-informed.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: 14 — Cross-Module Flows — forecast → MPS → MRP, sales → stock → accounts.

docs.title: Cross-Module Flows — Forecast → MPS → MRP, Sales → Stock → Accounts
What it does
docs.text: No module works alone. A sale consumes stock, stock triggers a purchase, a purchase posts to the ledger, and a forecast drives a production plan. This lesson is the map of how the modules connect — the three flows that run every real implementation. If you understand these, you can trace any number in the system back to the document that created it, and you can explain to a client why one wrong entry echoes through three modules.

docs.title: Core DocTypes
docs.text: DocType What it is Sales Forecast Expected demand per item, per period — the starting guess. Master Production Schedule The plan for what to make, by period, from the forecast and real orders. Production Plan The planner: turns the schedule and Sales Orders into Work Orders and Material Requests. Material Request (Manufacture) "We need these raw materials to produce." Raised by the Production Plan. Work Order The production order created from the plan. Purchase Order Buys the shortfall the plan found. Stock Entry Moves the materials and posts the finished goods. Sales Order The confirmed customer order — the other input to the plan. Delivery Note Ships the goods, moves stock out. Sales Invoice Books the revenue; the customer owes the money. Payment Entry Collects it.

docs.title: Flow 1 — forecast → MPS → MRP (planning)
docs.text:
Sales Forecast → Master Production Schedule → Production Plan
   (what we expect to sell)   (what we plan to make)   (what to order + make)
        → Material Request (Manufacture) → Purchase Order → Purchase Receipt
        → Work Order → Job Cards → Stock Entry (Manufacture) → finished stock
  • The Sales Forecast is a guess; the Master Production Schedule turns it into a make-plan by period; the Production Plan explodes it into real documents — Work Orders for what you make, Material Requests for what you need.
  • The plan checks available stock first. It only orders what is short. A plan run without accurate stock is a plan that orders what you already own.
  • MRP (Material Requirements Planning) is this explosion: demand minus stock minus on-order, per item, per date. The Production Plan is where ERPNext does it.

docs.title: Flow 2 — sales → stock → accounts (the daily loop)
docs.text:
Sales Order → Delivery Note (stock out) → Sales Invoice (revenue) → Payment Entry (cash)
     ↑                ↓
  reserves stock   Bin down, SLE written, ledger posted — one submit, three effects
  • One submit posts in three places: the Delivery Note moves stock, the Sales Invoice books revenue and the receivable, the Payment Entry clears it. That is why editing a submitted document is forbidden — the three records would disagree.
  • The same loop in reverse: Purchase Order → Purchase Receipt (stock in, value booked) → Purchase Invoice (liability) → Payment Entry.

docs.title: Flow 3 — production → QC → sales (the factory loop)
docs.text:
Work Order → Job Cards → Quality Inspection → finished stock → Delivery Note → invoice
   (make it)    (track it)   (prove it)        (sell it)
  • Production feeds Quality (lesson 06) and Quality gates Sales: a batch that fails inspection never reaches a Delivery Note.
  • Batch traceability ties the loop together: the pack a customer holds traces to the Work Order, the raw-material batch, the supplier and the inspection that passed it.

docs.title: Worked example — a spice manufacturer, one month
docs.text:
The fmc demo client (fmc) plans October:

  1. Sales Forecast: 2,000 kg chilli powder for October, from last year's sales plus the new distributor's order.
  2. Master Production Schedule: make 2,000 kg, 500 kg per week.
  3. Production Plan runs: stock on hand is 300 kg, so it creates Work Orders for 1,700 kg and Material Requests for 1,800 kg raw chilli (allowing process loss). The requests become Purchase Orders.
  4. Raw chilli arrives (Purchase Receipt → Quality Inspection → accepted into the raw store). Work Orders run weekly; Job Cards log grinding and packing; Stock Entry (Manufacture) books 490 kg per 500 kg batch.
  5. Distributor orders ship: Delivery Note (FEFO — oldest batch first) → Sales Invoice → Payment Entry. The ledger shows revenue; the stock report shows what is left; the plan for November starts from the real numbers, not a guess.

docs.title: A real use case
docs.text:
A manufacturer planned in Excel: the planner guessed demand, purchasing bought from the guess, and production ran out of one raw material while another piled up. After forecast → MPS → MRP in ERPNext, the plan ran from real orders and real stock — one material stopped expiring in the store, and the "we are out of chilli" emergency disappeared from the weekly meeting.

How we can use it: pitch the planning chain (forecast → MPS → MRP) to every textile, food and spare-parts manufacturer who still plans in Excel — it is the v16 feature that justifies the upgrade, and the demo (forecast in, Work Orders and Purchase Orders out) closes the sale. The sales → stock → accounts loop is the first flow to teach every new user: one submit, three effects.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Planning from a stale forecast. A forecast never updated is a plan built on last quarter's guess. Refresh it monthly.
  • Running the plan with wrong stock. The plan trusts Bin. If stock is wrong, the plan orders wrong — fix stock first (Stock Reconciliation).
  • Treating modules as separate systems. A "stock problem" is often a sales problem (no Sales Order) or a buying problem (no Purchase Receipt). Trace the flow, don't patch the symptom.
  • Skipping QC in the factory loop. A batch that fails inspection after delivery is a recall; before delivery it is a rework.
  • Forgetting the loop is the audit trail. Every number in a report comes from a document. If a number is wrong, find the document — never edit the report.

docs.title: 01 — What Frappe Is: Framework vs ERPNext vs Frappe Cloud
What it is
docs.text:
Three different things share the name "Frappe". Mixing them up is the first mistake most beginners make.

Frappe Framework — the platform. A full-stack web framework in Python and JavaScript, on MariaDB, Redis and Node.js. It gives you, out of the box:

  • DocTypes — one definition that creates the database table, the form, the list view, the API and the permissions.
  • Desk — the admin UI your users work in every day.
  • REST API, background jobs, scheduler, workflows, reports, print formats, email and notifications — all built in, no extra libraries to wire up.

The Framework is MIT-licensed and open source. Current version: v16, with monthly releases (16.60, 16.61, …). Since v16.60, Studio (no-code app builder) and Flow (AI in Desk) ship inside the Framework itself.

ERPNext — the business app built on Frappe. Accounting, Stock, Selling, Buying, Manufacturing, HR, CRM, Projects, Assets, Helpdesk. It is one app that runs on a Frappe site, the same way your own custom app does. GPL-3.0 licensed. When someone says "we run ERPNext", they mean a Frappe site with the ERPNext app installed.

Frappe Cloud — hosted Frappe. Your sites run on Frappe's infrastructure. You deploy custom apps from a Git repo through the dashboard. There is no shell access, and no Server Scripts on shared benches. You trade control for zero server work.

Other Frappe apps follow the same pattern: HRMS, CRM, Helpdesk, Insights, Raven, Builder, Wiki, Drive — each is an app you install on a site.

One-line mental model: Framework is the engine, ERPNext is the car built on it, Frappe Cloud is renting the car with a driver.

docs.title: How the pieces fit
docs.text:
bench  (a folder on your machine or server)
 ├── apps/      frappe, erpnext, my_app, hrms, ...
 └── sites/     site1.local, client-a.com, ...
                 └── each site = one database + files

One bench holds many sites. One site runs many apps. A document (a Sales Order, an Employee, a custom record) always belongs to one site.

docs.title: When to use which
docs.text: Goal Use Learn to build, or build a custom app Framework on a local bench Run a business end to end ERPNext (Cloud or self-hosted) Client wants zero server work Frappe Cloud Need shell access, custom infra, local-only data rules Self-hosted bench Build a product to sell Custom app on Framework (plus ERPNext if it extends the ERP) Quick prototype for one client Framework + Studio (v16.60+) before writing code

docs.title: Minimal example — see it yourself
docs.text:
On a bench that already has ERPNext installed:

bench --version        # the bench CLI version
bench list-apps        # apps on this bench: frappe, erpnext, ...
bench --site mysite.local list-apps   # apps installed on one site

Then open http://mysite.local:8000 and sign in as Administrator:

  • Search "Company" in the top search bar — that is an ERPNext DocType.
  • Search "DocType" — that is the Framework's own list of DocTypes.
  • Search "Sales Invoice" — ERPNext again. Every screen you see is a DocType rendered by the Framework.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Thinking ERPNext is Frappe. ERPNext is one app. The Framework is the platform everything runs on. You can run Frappe with no ERPNext at all.
  • Editing ERPNext's files directly. Never edit another app's code. Extend it from your own app with hooks, overrides and fixtures instead.
  • Self-hosting for a small client who just needs ERPNext. A server plus your maintenance time costs more than Frappe Cloud for most small sites.
  • Choosing Cloud when the client needs shell-level work — custom system packages, local-only data, or direct database access. Cloud has no shell.
  • Starting with code before checking what already exists. ERPNext, HRMS, CRM and the Apps Catalog already solve most requirements. Build only the gap.

docs.title: Key terms — keep these
docs.text:
• DocType — the definition of a record type (table + form + list + rules).
  • Document — one record (one Sales Order, one Employee).
  • Desk — the web UI.
  • bench — the CLI and folder that holds apps and sites.
  • site — one database + one set of installed apps.
  • app — a package of DocTypes, code and fixtures (frappe, erpnext, yours).
  • docstatus — 0 Draft, 1 Submitted, 2 Cancelled. You will meet it in every ERPNext lesson.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: 02 — Bench, sites & apps — install it and create your first site and app.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
bench is the command-line tool that creates and manages everything: the bench folder, the apps inside it, and the sites that run on it.

  • A bench is a folder. It holds apps/, sites/, config/ and env/.
  • A site is one database plus its files. One bench can hold many sites.
  • An app is a package of DocTypes, Python/JS code and fixtures. Apps live in apps/ and are installed on a site before they do anything.

docs.title: Prerequisites (v16)
docs.text:
Item Version Python 3.14 Node.js 24+ (plus Yarn 1.22+) MariaDB 11.8 documented (10.6 works in practice) Redis required — caching, queues, realtime

Install bench itself with uv (the current official method):

uv tool install frappe-bench
bench --version

docs.title: Minimal working example — from zero to a running site
docs.text:
# 1. Create a bench on the v16 branch
bench init --frappe-branch version-16 frappe-bench
cd frappe-bench

# 2. Download ERPNext (same major version as Frappe — never mix v15 and v16)
bench get-app --branch version-16 erpnext

# 3. Create a site and install ERPNext on it in one step
bench new-site mysite.local --install-app erpnext
#    (prompts for the MariaDB root password, then the Administrator password)

# 4. Create your own app
bench new-app my_app
#    (prompts for title, description, publisher, email, licence)

# 5. Install your app on the site
bench --site mysite.local install-app my_app

# 6. Start everything
bench start
#    Open http://mysite.local:8000 — sign in as Administrator

What each command did:

Command What it does bench init Creates the bench folder, installs Frappe into it bench get-app Downloads an app into apps/ — does not install it anywhere yet bench new-site Creates a new database + site folder; --install-app installs the app right away bench new-app Scaffolds a new custom app in apps/ bench --site X install-app Activates an app on one site (creates its tables) bench start Runs the web server, workers and scheduler for development

Useful everyday commands:

bench use mysite.local                 # make this the default site (skip --site)
bench list-apps                        # apps on the bench
bench --site mysite.local list-apps    # apps installed on one site
bench --site mysite.local migrate      # apply DocType / patch / fixture changes
bench --site mysite.local backup --with-files --compress
bench --site mysite.local console      # Python shell inside the site
bench --site mysite.local clear-cache  # after hooks.py changes
bench --site mysite.local enable-scheduler

docs.title: When to use which command
docs.text:
• New project → bench init, then bench new-app, then a site.
  • New client site on an existing bench → bench new-site only.
  • Add ERPNext / HRMS / CRM to a site → bench get-app (once per bench), then bench --site … install-app (once per site).
  • You changed a DocType, a patch or a fixture → bench migrate.
  • You changed public JS/CSS → bench build --app my_app.
  • You changed hooks.py → bench clear-cache.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Running bench as root. Use a dedicated frappe user. Never sudo bench.
  • Mixing major versions. Frappe v16 + ERPNext v15 (or the reverse) breaks. Pin both with --branch version-16.
  • Forgetting migrate. DocType JSON, patches and fixtures only apply on bench --site … migrate. If your new field is missing, migrate first.
  • Deleting an app folder by hand. Use bench remove-app — it also removes the database tables. A hand-deleted folder leaves a broken site.
  • No backup before update / migrate / restore. Back up first, and test a restore on a staging site at least once — a backup you never restored is not a backup.
  • One bench, one site, forever. Benches are cheap. Keep dev, staging and production on separate benches (or separate servers), never on one site.
  • Running production on bench start. That is the development server. Production uses nginx + supervisor (bench setup production) or Docker.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text: After the example above you should be able to answer: which apps are on the bench, which are installed on mysite.local, and what bench start printed. If the site does not open, check the terminal output first — the error is usually a wrong MariaDB password or a port already in use.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: 03 — Your first DocType — define a record type with fields, types and a clean layout.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A DocType is the definition of a record type. One definition gives you five things at once: the database table, the form, the list view, the REST API, and the permissions. If you can define a DocType well, you can build most of Frappe.

Every DocType is a JSON file in your app:

my_app/
  my_app/doctype/gate_pass/gate_pass.json   # the definition
  my_app/doctype/gate_pass/gate_pass.py     # server logic (controller)
  my_app/doctype/gate_pass/gate_pass.js     # form behaviour (UX only)

docs.title: Minimal working example — a Gate Pass
docs.text:
A factory needs a gate pass: who came, for which company, why, and what they carried in or out. Create it in the UI first (Desk → search "DocType" → New), with Module set to your app and developer_mode on, so the JSON is saved into your app.

Fields — in this order:

# Fieldname Label Type Notes 1 naming_series Series Select Options: GP-.YYYY.-.#### 2 gate_pass_date Date Date Default: Today 3 visitor_name Visitor Data Required 4 company Company Link Options: Company 5 purpose Purpose Select Visit / Delivery / Pickup 6 section_break_1 Details Section Break starts the items section 7 items Items Table Options: Gate Pass Item 8 remarks Remarks Small Text

The child table Gate Pass Item (its own DocType, marked "Is Child Table"):

Fieldname Label Type Notes item_name Item Data In List View qty Qty Int In List View direction Direction Select In / Out

Naming: set Autoname to naming_series. The first pass becomes GP-2026-0001. If you leave Autoname blank, Frappe names records by a hash nobody can read — always set it.

After creating it in the UI, apply it to the site:

bench --site mysite.local migrate

Then open Gate Pass → New in Desk and create one. You have just built a working app screen with zero code.

docs.title: Field types you will use most
docs.text:
Type For Example Data short text visitor name Link a record in another DocType Company, Customer, Item Select fixed list of options purpose, status Date / Datetime dates pass date, due date Currency / Float / Int numbers amount, qty, rate Check yes/no is active Text / Small Text longer text remarks, address Table child rows items, taxes Attach / Attach Image files CNIC copy, photo Section Break / Column Break / Tab Break layout only (no data stored)

Rule of thumb: if the value must match a master record, use Link, never free text. Free text for a company name means ten spellings of the same company later.

docs.title: Layout rules — read these before adding any field
docs.text:
Bad field layout is the most common beginner mistake. These five rules come from real projects (see guides/common-mistakes.md):

  1. Read the form first. Open the existing form before adding a field. Add to the flow that is already there — do not bolt fields on at the end.
  2. Place with insert_after. Every new field names the field it goes after. Fields without a position land at the bottom in a pile.
