  3. Two fields per row. A row is: field, Column Break, field, then a Section Break starts the next row. Never stack six fields in one column — the form becomes a long, unreadable scroll.
  4. A child table gets its own section. Put a Section Break before it, with a clear label ("Items"). A table squeezed between two data fields looks broken and is easy to miss.
  5. Max 4–5 columns in List View. Only tick In List View for the fields a user scans to find a record. Everything else belongs on the form.

Applied to the Gate Pass: Section 1 holds series, date, visitor, company, purpose (two per row); Section 2 ("Items") holds only the table; remarks sit in their own row at the end.

docs.title: When to use a DocType vs a Custom Field
docs.text:
• New record type (Gate Pass, Sample Request, Service Ticket) → new DocType in your app.
  • One extra field on someone else's DocType (a "Transporter" field on Delivery Note) → Custom Field, exported as a fixture — never edit the other app's DocType JSON.
  • One-off field on your own DocType → add it to the DocType, in the right position, following the five rules above.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• No Section / Column Breaks. One long column of 20 fields. Users hate it, and it is the first thing a reviewer will flag.
  • Free text where a Link belongs. "Customer" as Data instead of Link to Customer — reports and filters break.
  • Child table without its own section. It renders cramped and gets missed.
  • Everything In List View. Ten columns in the list, half of them empty. Keep it to 4–5.
  • No naming series. Records named by hash are unfindable on the phone.
  • Creating the DocType in the wrong module. It lands in the wrong app and cannot be shipped. Set Module before you start.
  • Skipping migrate. The DocType exists in the UI but the table is not created until you migrate.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: 04 — Desk, List View, Form View — how users actually work with the records you just defined.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: Desk is the web UI every Frappe user lives in. It has three parts you need to understand: the Workspace (the home screen), the List View (find records), and the Form View (work on one record). Your DocType automatically gets all three — your job is to make them usable.

docs.title: The Desk shell
docs.text:
• Sidebar — modules and workspaces. Workspaces group the DocTypes, reports and dashboards one role needs. A workspace without a Module set is visible to every Desk user — set the module, and restrict finance/HR workspaces by role.
  • Search bar (Awesomebar) — type a DocType, a document name, or a report and jump straight to it. This is how experienced users navigate; the sidebar is for discovery.
  • Notifications & assignments — the bell, and the "Assigned To" list on forms. Work comes to the user instead of the user hunting for it.
  • The user menu (top right) — "About" shows the versions the site runs.

docs.title: List View — finding and triaging
docs.text:
The List View answers one question: which records need attention?

  • Columns come from fields marked In List View (max 4–5 — see Lesson 03). They are what a user scans. Pick the fields that identify a record: name, date, party, status, amount.
  • Filters — filter by status, date, company, owner. Save a filter as a named view ("My open orders", "Overdue invoices") so the team shares it.
  • Sort — newest first is the default for transactions; change it when the job needs oldest-first (for example, oldest unpaid invoice).
  • Views — List, Report, Kanban (by status), Calendar, Gantt, Tree. Kanban is the right view for a pipeline (leads, support tickets); the plain list is right for triage.
  • Bulk actions — select rows and Assign, print, export or delete in bulk.
  • List Settings (the gear icon) — pick which columns show, without code.

A good list lets a user find a record in seconds and see its state at a glance. A bad list is 12 columns wide, unfiltered, and sorted wrong.

docs.title: Form View — working on one record
docs.text:
The Form View answers: what is this record, and what do I do with it?

  • Sections and tabs — the layout you defined in the DocType. Sections group related fields; tabs split a long form (Details / Items / Terms).
  • Child tables — rows inside the form (items, taxes). They have their own section and their own columns.
  • Status bar — Draft / Submitted / Cancelled (docstatus), plus the workflow state when a Workflow is active.
  • Save / Submit / Cancel / Amend — Save keeps a Draft editable. Submit locks it and posts its effects (stock moves, GL entries). Cancel reverses them. Amend creates a new Draft linked to the cancelled one. Never edit a submitted document's fields directly.
  • Timeline — every comment, assignment, attachment and version change, in order. This is the audit trail — it is why "just call me" is not a process.
  • Actions menu — Print, Email, Share, Duplicate, and "New" for a linked document (for example, a Sales Invoice from a Sales Order).
  • Customize (in developer mode) — add a field or change a label from the form itself. Handy for a quick fix; ship it as a fixture afterwards.

docs.title: Minimal example — a morning's work in Desk
docs.text:
You are the sales user. It is 9 a.m.

  1. Open the Selling workspace — your quotations and orders are there.
  2. Open Sales Order → List, filter Status = "To Deliver", sort by Delivery Date. The overdue ones are on top.
  3. Open the first order. The form shows the customer, items, taxes, and the status bar ("To Deliver and Bill").
  4. From the actions menu, create the Delivery Note. Submit it — stock moves out. The timeline records who did it and when.
  5. Back in the list, the order now reads "To Bill". Create the Sales Invoice the same way. Done — the order is "Completed".

No code was written. That whole flow is DocTypes, lists and forms doing their job.

docs.title: When to use which view
docs.text: Job View Find a record List, with a filter See what is overdue / pending List, sorted and filtered Work a pipeline (leads, tickets) Kanban Enter or check one record Form See everything that happened to a record Form → Timeline Export for a meeting List → Report view or Export

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating the list as the place to edit. The list is for finding. Edit on the form — that is where validation, permissions and the timeline live.
  • Too many list columns. More than 4–5 and nobody can scan the list.
  • No saved filters. Every user re-builds "my open orders" daily. Save the filter once, share it with the role.
  • Hiding a field in JS to "secure" it. Hiding is not security — anyone can read the field through the API. Use permlevel (field-level permission) instead.
  • Working from memory instead of the timeline. If it is not in the timeline, it did not happen. Comments and assignments belong on the document.
  • One workspace for everyone. A sales user does not need the payroll workspace. Workspaces are per role, not per site.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: You have finished Level 1. You can explain Frappe, run a bench, define a DocType with a clean layout, and work in Desk. Level 2 starts with Server Scripts & Document Events — where the logic belongs.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Server-side logic is the logic that must run — validation, totals, status changes, creating linked records. It runs on the server, so no one can bypass it from the browser or the API. There are three places it can live, and picking the wrong one is the most common Level 2 mistake:

Where For Controller (gate_pass.py) Logic on a DocType your own app owns Server Script (Desk → Server Script) A quick rule, no app deploy needed doc_events in hooks.py Logic on another app's DocType (Sales Order, Delivery Note)

The controller runs at fixed points in a document's life — the hooks:

Hook When it runs before_insert Before a new document is saved the first time validate Before every save (this is "Before Save") before_save After validate, before the save writes on_update After every save before_submit / on_submit Around submit (posting happens here) before_cancel / on_cancel Around cancel (reversals happen here) on_trash Before delete

docs.title: Minimal working example — Gate Pass controller
docs.text:
First, tick Is Submittable on the Gate Pass DocType from Lesson 03, so Submit exists. Then the controller:

# my_app/my_module/doctype/gate_pass/gate_pass.py
import frappe
from frappe import _
from frappe.model.document import Document


class GatePass(Document):
    def validate(self):
        # Delivery / Pickup passes must list what is carried
        if self.purpose in ("Delivery", "Pickup") and not self.items:
            frappe.throw(
                _("Add at least one item for a {0} pass").format(self.purpose)
            )
        for row in self.items:
            if row.qty <= 0:
                frappe.throw(
                    _("Row {0}: Qty must be greater than 0").format(row.idx)
                )

    def on_submit(self):
        # A reminder for whoever submitted it — created by the system
        frappe.get_doc({
            "doctype": "ToDo",
            "description": _("Gate Pass {0} for {1} submitted").format(
                self.name, self.visitor_name
            ),
            "reference_type": self.doctype,
            "reference_name": self.name,
            "allocated_to": frappe.session.user,
            "status": "Open",
        }).insert(ignore_permissions=True)  # system-created, not a user action

Rules inside validate / before_save: set fields on self directly, never call self.save(). Inside on_update / on_submit, if you must change your own fields, use self.db_set("field", value). Use frappe.utils helpers (flt, getdate, add_days, date_diff) — never float() / int() on doc fields, which may be None.

docs.title: Same rule, no code deploy — a Server Script
docs.text:
Desk → search Server Script → New. Type: Document Event, Document Type: Sales Order, DocType Event: Before Save:

# No import statements — frappe and frappe.utils are pre-loaded
if doc.delivery_date and frappe.utils.date_diff(doc.delivery_date, frappe.utils.today()) < 0:
    frappe.throw(_("Delivery Date cannot be in the past"))

Server Scripts run in a RestrictedPython sandbox: no import, no raise (use frappe.throw), and try/except is blocked on v14–v15 — use if checks such as frappe.db.exists(). On v15+ they are disabled by default; enable with bench set-config -g server_script_enabled 1. Not available on Frappe Cloud shared benches.

Event name trap: in a Server Script, "Before Save" is the validate hook, not before_save. "After Save" is on_update, "Before Submit" is before_submit, "After Submit" is on_submit.

docs.title: Same rule, another app's DocType — doc_events
docs.text:
Your app does not own Sales Order, so you do not touch its controller. You register a hook in hooks.py — a registry only, no logic in it:

# hooks.py
doc_events = {
    "Sales Order": {
        "validate": "my_app.selling.overrides.sales_order.validate",
    },
}

# my_app/selling/overrides/sales_order.py
import frappe
from frappe import _


def validate(doc, method=None):
    if frappe.db.get_value("Customer", doc.customer, "disabled"):
        frappe.throw(
            _("Customer {0} is disabled").format(frappe.bold(doc.customer))
        )

docs.title: When to use — and when not to
docs.text: Situation Use Logic on your own DocType Controller method (validate, on_submit, …) One quick rule, no app release yet Server Script Logic on ERPNext's DocType doc_events in hooks.py → override file in your app Rule over 50 lines, needs imports or tests Controller — never a Server Script Showing/hiding a field, a button, a hint Client Script (Lesson 06), not the server Calling an external API on_update / on_submit + frappe.enqueue — never in validate

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Logic inside hooks.py. It is a registry of dotted paths. The code lives in the file the path points to.
  • doc_events for a DocType your own app owns. Use the controller — no hooks entry is needed at all.
  • "*" doc_events. It runs on every save of every DocType, forever.
  • Validation only in JS. JS is UX (Lesson 06). A rule enforced in JS alone is not a rule — the API bypasses it.
  • Submit-only work in validate. validate runs on every save, including drafts. Posting and ledger work belongs in on_submit.
  • Calling self.save() inside validate. You are already inside a save. Set fields on self and return.
  • Editing another app's files. Never edit apps/erpnext/... — the next update wipes it. Extend from your app.
  • A Server Script that grew into an app. Over 50 lines, external libraries, or tests needed? Move it to a controller.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: 06 — Client Scripts — form behaviour, validation hints, and UX. What belongs in the browser, and what must stay on the server.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A Client Script is JavaScript that runs in the user's browser, on the form. It controls behaviour and experience: show or hide a field, make a field mandatory, filter a Link, add a button, fetch a value and show it. It is UX only — it is not security and not validation. Anything the browser can do, the API can skip.

For a DocType your app owns, the script lives with the DocType:

my_app/doctype/gate_pass/gate_pass.js   # form behaviour for Gate Pass

For another app's DocType (Sales Order, Delivery Note), use the Client Script DocType in Desk, or doctype_js in hooks.py pointing at a file in public/js/. Never duplicate the same frappe.ui.form.on block for one DocType — extend the existing handler.

docs.title: Minimal working example — Gate Pass form
docs.text:
// gate_pass.js
frappe.ui.form.on("Gate Pass", {
    setup(frm) {
        // set_query belongs here — it runs once per form load
        frm.set_query("company", () => ({ filters: { disabled: 0 } }));
    },

    refresh(frm) {
        // Items are mandatory for Delivery / Pickup, optional for Visit
        frm.toggle_reqd("items", ["Delivery", "Pickup"].includes(frm.doc.purpose));
        if (frm.doc.docstatus === 1) {
            frm.add_custom_button(__("Mark Returned"), () => {
                frappe.call({
                    method: "my_app.gate_pass.api.mark_returned",
                    args: { name: frm.doc.name },
                    callback() { frm.reload_doc(); },
                });
            }, __("Actions"));
        }
    },

    purpose(frm) {
        // Runs whenever the Purpose field changes
        frm.toggle_reqd("items", ["Delivery", "Pickup"].includes(frm.doc.purpose));
        frm.refresh_field("items");
    },

    validate(frm) {
        // A UX hint only — the server re-checks this in validate() (Lesson 05)
        if (["Delivery", "Pickup"].includes(frm.doc.purpose) && !frm.doc.items.length) {
            frappe.msgprint(__("Add at least one item for a Delivery or Pickup pass"));
        }
    },
});

The server side the button needs (Lesson 07 has the full pattern):

# my_app/gate_pass/api.py
import frappe


@frappe.whitelist()
def mark_returned(name):
    doc = frappe.get_doc("Gate Pass", name)
    doc.check_permission("write")
    doc.db_set("status", "Returned")

The Gate Pass needs a status field for this to work — add a Select (Open / Returned, default Open) to the DocType from Lesson 03.

docs.title: The form events you will use most
When to use — and when not to
docs.text: Situation Use Show/hide a field, make it mandatory Client Script (toggle_display, toggle_reqd) Filter a Link field's options frm.set_query in setup Copy a field from a linked document Fetch From on the field in the DocType — not JS Static visibility / mandatory rules Depends On / Mandatory Depends On in the DocType — not JS A button that does server work frm.add_custom_button + frappe.call to a whitelisted method A rule that must hold Server validate() (Lesson 05) — JS may only hint at it Reading data that rarely changes Load once in onload — do not call the server from refresh

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Validation only in JS. The API bypasses the form entirely. Every rule that matters lives in the controller.
  • set_query in refresh or a field event. It runs on every render. Put it in setup.
  • Hiding a field in JS to "secure" it. Anyone can read the field through the API. Use permlevel — Lesson 09.
  • cur_frm. Use the frm argument the event gives you.
  • Two frappe.ui.form.on blocks for the same DocType in one file. Extend the one handler.
  • Direct DOM manipulation ($(...) on form fields) when a frm.* API exists (set_value, set_df_property, toggle_display).
  • Synchronous server calls (async: false). Use promises (.then) or async/await.
  • Saving through the API for the open form. Use frm.set_value, then frm.save() — never frappe.client.set_value on the open form.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: 07 — APIs — frappe.call, whitelisted methods, and the REST API. How the browser, other systems, and your own code talk to the server.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Every DocType already has an API — the form, the list and the REST API are all the same server underneath. There are three ways to call it:

Way From For frm.call("method") The open form A method on the current document's controller frappe.call({ method: "app.module.file.fn" }) Any form JS A module-level whitelisted function REST: /api/resource/..., /api/method/... Any system, curl, Postman Other apps and integrations

A Python function is callable from outside only if it has @frappe.whitelist(). Without the decorator, the call is a 403. And every whitelisted function is a public endpoint — it must check permissions before returning data, not after.

docs.title: Minimal working example — check available stock
docs.text:
A whitelisted function in your app:

# my_app/stock/api.py
import frappe


@frappe.whitelist()
def get_available_qty(item_code, warehouse):
    frappe.has_permission("Bin", "read", throw=True)
    qty = frappe.db.get_value(
        "Bin",
        {"item_code": item_code, "warehouse": warehouse},
        "actual_qty",
    )
    return qty or 0

Call it from a Sales Order form — a "Check Stock" button:

frm.add_custom_button(__("Check Stock"), () => {
    const row = (frm.doc.items || [])[0];
    if (!row) return;
    frappe.call({
        method: "my_app.stock.api.get_available_qty",
        args: { item_code: row.item_code, warehouse: row.warehouse },
        callback(r) {
            frappe.msgprint(__("Available qty: {0}", [r.message]));
        },
    });
}, __("Actions"));

Call the same logic from outside Frappe, over REST. First create a dedicated API user with minimal roles (never use Administrator keys), then generate its keys (User → API Access → Generate Keys):

# Read one Sales Order
curl "https://mysite.local/api/resource/Sales%20Order/SAL-ORD-2026-00001" \
  -H "Authorization: token <api_key>:<api_secret>" \
  -H "Accept: application/json"

# Call the whitelisted method over REST
curl -X POST "https://mysite.local/api/method/my_app.stock.api.get_available_qty" \
  -H "Authorization: token <api_key>:<api_secret>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"item_code": "SPICE-MIX-01", "warehouse": "Stores - NT"}'

GET /api/resource/<DocType> lists records, GET .../<name> reads one, POST creates, PUT updates, DELETE deletes. Test a whitelisted method from the bench without any HTTP at all:

bench --site mysite.local execute my_app.stock.api.get_available_qty \
  --args '["SPICE-MIX-01", "Stores - NT"]'

docs.title: When to use — and when not to
docs.text: Situation Use Logic for the document open on screen frm.call to a controller method Logic shared by several forms / DocTypes Module-level @frappe.whitelist() + frappe.call Another system reads or writes Frappe data REST /api/resource/... with a dedicated API user Another system needs one custom operation REST /api/method/... to a whitelisted function Anything that writes POST, with methods=["POST"] on the decorator Calling an external API from Frappe on_update / on_submit + frappe.enqueue, with a timeout — never in validate A guest (logged-out) user needs data allow_guest=True only for reads, with input validation — never for writes

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• No permission check. A whitelisted method without frappe.has_permission(..., throw=True) (or doc.check_permission) hands data to anyone who can guess the URL.
  • Missing @frappe.whitelist(). The call fails with 403 and the method works fine in Python — the decorator is what exposes it.
  • GET for a write. State changes go through POST. A GET that writes can be triggered by a link, a prefetch, or a retry.
  • Administrator API keys. Keys belong to a user, and that user has that user's roles. A dedicated API user with minimal roles limits the damage if a key leaks.
  • Secrets in JS or hardcoded. API keys and passwords go in a Settings Single DocType with a Password field (doc.get_password("api_key")) or frappe.conf — never in client code.
  • No timeout on outbound calls. requests.post(url, json=..., timeout=30), wrapped in try/except, errors in frappe.log_error. A hung external API must never hang a save.
  • Returning whole documents from an API. Return the fields the caller needs — a full doc leaks fields the caller should not see.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: 08 — Reports & Print Formats — Script Reports, Query Reports, and Jinja print formats. Turning the data your API just returned into something a manager can read.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A report answers a question over many records ("which gate passes are still open this month?"). A print format renders one document for paper or PDF ("the gate pass itself"). Pick the report type first:

Type For Report Builder (no code) A filtered list of one DocType — prefer it when it is enough Query Report One SQL query, no Python logic Script Report Logic, several sources, computed columns — the default for custom reports

A standard report lives in your app, so it is versioned:

my_app/my_module/report/gate_pass_register/
  gate_pass_register.json   # the Report definition
  gate_pass_register.py     # execute(filters) -> columns, data
  gate_pass_register.js     # filters

docs.title: Minimal working example — Gate Pass Register (Script Report)
docs.text:
# gate_pass_register.py
import frappe
from frappe import _


def execute(filters=None):
    filters = frappe._dict(filters or {})
    validate_filters(filters)
    return get_columns(), get_data(filters)


def validate_filters(filters):
    if filters.from_date and filters.to_date and filters.from_date > filters.to_date:
        frappe.throw(_("From Date cannot be after To Date"))


def get_columns():
    return [
        {"label": _("Gate Pass"), "fieldname": "name", "fieldtype": "Link", "options": "Gate Pass", "width": 140},
        {"label": _("Date"), "fieldname": "gate_pass_date", "fieldtype": "Date", "width": 110},
        {"label": _("Visitor"), "fieldname": "visitor_name", "fieldtype": "Data", "width": 160},
        {"label": _("Company"), "fieldname": "company", "fieldtype": "Link", "options": "Company", "width": 160},
        {"label": _("Purpose"), "fieldname": "purpose", "fieldtype": "Data", "width": 100},
    ]


def get_data(filters):
    query_filters = {}
    if filters.get("company"):
        query_filters["company"] = filters.company
    if filters.get("purpose"):
        query_filters["purpose"] = filters.purpose
    if filters.get("from_date") and filters.get("to_date"):
        query_filters["gate_pass_date"] = ("between", [filters.from_date, filters.to_date])
    elif filters.get("from_date"):
        query_filters["gate_pass_date"] = (">=", filters.from_date)
    elif filters.get("to_date"):
        query_filters["gate_pass_date"] = ("<=", filters.to_date)
    return frappe.get_list(
        "Gate Pass",
        filters=query_filters,
        fields=["name", "gate_pass_date", "visitor_name", "company", "purpose"],
        order_by="gate_pass_date desc",
    )

// gate_pass_register.js
frappe.query_reports["Gate Pass Register"] = {
    filters: [
        { fieldname: "from_date", label: __("From Date"), fieldtype: "Date", default: frappe.datetime.month_start(), reqd: 1 },
        { fieldname: "to_date", label: __("To Date"), fieldtype: "Date", default: frappe.datetime.month_end(), reqd: 1 },
        { fieldname: "company", label: __("Company"), fieldtype: "Link", options: "Company" },
        { fieldname: "purpose", label: __("Purpose"), fieldtype: "Select", options: "\nVisit\nDelivery\nPickup" },
    ],
};

Columns are dicts with a real fieldtype (Currency, Link, Date) — not "Customer:Link/Customer:180" strings in new code. Filters are applied in the query, not in Python. frappe.get_list respects permissions; frappe.db.sql bypasses all permission checks — never use it for user-facing reads.

docs.title: Minimal example — a Print Format (Jinja)
docs.text:
Desk → Print Format → New, DocType: Gate Pass, Print Format Type: Jinja. The template gets doc (the document) and frappe:

<h2>Gate Pass {{ doc.name }}</h2>
<p>{{ _("Date") }}: {{ doc.get_formatted("gate_pass_date") }}
  {{ _("Visitor") }}: {{ doc.visitor_name }}</p>
<table>
  <tr><th>{{ _("Item") }}</th><th>{{ _("Qty") }}</th><th>{{ _("Direction") }}</th></tr>
  {% for row in doc.items %}
  <tr><td>{{ row.item_name }}</td><td>{{ row.qty }}</td><td>{{ row.direction }}</td></tr>
  {% endfor %}
</table>

Use doc.get_formatted("field") for currency and dates, _() for labels, and keep database calls out of loops (frappe.db.get_value sparingly, never one per row). Prefer the Print Format Builder, or a Jinja format stored in your app as a standard print format, so it ships with the app.

docs.title: When to use — and when not to
docs.text: Situation Use A filtered list of one DocType Report Builder — no code at all One SQL query, fixed columns Query Report Logic, several DocTypes, computed values Script Report A document on paper / PDF Print Format (Builder first, Jinja when you need layout control) The same report for every client Standard report in the app (Is Standard = Yes, module set) A one-off question for one user Report Builder, or a saved filter on the List View — not a coded report

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• frappe.get_doc inside a loop (N+1). One query per row makes a 500-row report take 30 seconds. Fetch once, then look up in a dict (see guides/common-mistakes.md §4).
  • Filters applied in Python. Filter in the query — the database is faster than your loop, and it respects permissions.
  • frappe.db.sql for a user-facing report. It bypasses permissions. Use frappe.get_list, Query Builder, or a permission-aware query.
  • Columns as strings in new code. Use dicts with fieldtype — the report renders links, currency and dates correctly.
  • Database queries inside a Jinja loop. One get_value per row in a print format is the same N+1 mistake, on paper.
  • A coded report for a one-off question. If Report Builder answers it, ship nothing. Code is maintenance.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: 09 — Permissions & Roles — who can see, edit, submit, and print all of this. Role Permissions, field-level permissions, User Permissions, and sharing.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Access is granted only when every layer allows it. Four layers, in order — a failure at any one of them means "no":

  1. Role permission — what a role may do on a DocType (read, write, create, submit, cancel, print, export, report…).
  2. User Permission — which documents: a user restricted to one Company or Branch sees only that company's records.
  3. Sharing — one document, shared with one user, as an exception.
  4. has_permission hook — code that decides on one document.

Desk and /api/resource/... run the same checks. If it works in Desk but fails from the API, the API user (the token owner) lacks the role.

docs.title: Minimal working example — Gate Pass access
docs.text:
1. Role permissions — Desk → Role Permissions Manager, DocType: Gate Pass. Set Is Submittable on the DocType first (Lesson 05), then:

Role Read Write Create Submit Cancel Gate Security ✓ ✓ ✓ — — Store Manager ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Auditor ✓ — — — —

A role with no read permission cannot open the DocType at all — sharing one document does not fix that.

2. Field-level permission (permlevel). The remarks field holds internal notes. Set its Permlevel to 1 on the DocType, then in Role Permissions Manager give level 1 read only to Store Manager. Gate Security sees the form — without the remarks field.

3. User Permission — one gate user sees only one company:

frappe.permissions.add_user_permission("Company", "NexTash Pvt Ltd", "gate.security@example.com")

It filters lists, links and reports. A user who sees an empty list usually has a User Permission hiding the documents, not a missing share.

4. Sharing — one document, one user, as an exception:

frappe.share.add("Gate Pass", "GP-2026-0001", "auditor@example.com", read=1)
frappe.share.remove("Gate Pass", "GP-2026-0001", "auditor@example.com")

Sharing grants access to that one document only. It does not replace the role permission — the user still needs read on the DocType. Routine access belongs in roles, not in shares.

Check in code the same way the framework does:

frappe.has_permission("Gate Pass", "read", doc, throw=True)

docs.title: When to use — and when not to
docs.text: Situation Use A whole team needs a DocType Role permission (Role Permissions Manager) One user must see only one Company / Branch User Permission One document for one outside person, once Sharing A rule code must decide ("only the owner, or a manager") has_permission hook — on v16 it must return an explicit True; returning None denies access Hiding a field from a role permlevel — never JS A report or page for one role only Role Permission for Page and Report

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Hiding a field in JS is not security. Anyone can read the field through the API. Use permlevel.
  • ignore_permissions=True without a reason. If you pass it, write the reason in a comment next to it — otherwise the next developer copies it everywhere.
  • allow_guest=True on anything that writes. Guest endpoints are read-only, rate-limited, and must validate every input.
  • has_permission returning None on v16. On v14/v15 None meant "no opinion"; on v16 it denies access. Return True explicitly.
  • Sharing is not a role. Sharing one document gives access to that one document only. The user still needs read on the DocType.
  • Whitelisted methods check permission last. Check with frappe.has_permission(..., throw=True) before returning data, not after (Lesson 07).
  • frappe.db.sql for user-facing reads. It bypasses every permission layer. Use frappe.get_list / frappe.get_all, which apply User Permissions automatically.

403? Check in this order: role permission on the DocType → User Permission hiding the document → has_permission hook returning None or False → whitelisted method missing the decorator or the check → the API token's user lacking the role.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: 10 — Workflows & Assignments — approvals and automatic routing. Who may move a document forward, and who it lands with.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A Workflow is a state machine for a document: who may move it from one stage to the next, and under what condition. An Assignment Rule routes the document to a person automatically — round robin, least busy, or from a field on the document itself. Together they answer: who approves this, and whose desk does it land on?

A Workflow only works on a submittable DocType (is_submittable) — it drives docstatus (0 Draft, 1 Submitted, 2 Cancelled), so there must be a submitted state to drive. When you activate a Workflow, Frappe creates the workflow_state field on the DocType for you — do not drive state with a custom Select field.

docs.title: Minimal working example — Quality Inspection approval
docs.text:
A spice batch arrives. The inspection must be approved by the QA Manager before the batch can be used. Desk → Workflow → New, Document Type: Quality Inspection, Is Active ✓.

States — each state carries a docstatus:

State Doc Status Who can edit Draft 0 Quality User Pending Approval 0 — Approved 1 — Rejected 0 Quality User

Transitions — each one: from a state, an action, to a state, a role, an optional condition:

From Action To Allowed Condition Draft Submit for Approval Pending Approval Quality User Pending Approval Approve Approved Quality Manager Pending Approval Reject Rejected Quality Manager Rejected Revise Draft Quality User

Two rules that save real projects:

  • Intermediate approval states stay at docstatus 0. Only the final "Approved" state is 1. A submitted document cannot go back to draft — docstatus only moves forward (0→0, 0→1, 1→1, 1→2).
  • Rejected is docstatus 0, so it can be fixed and resubmitted. A rejected inspection that is docstatus 1 or 2 is stuck.

Set Allow Self Approval = 0 when the creator must not approve their own document. Only one Workflow per DocType can be active. Conditions are Python expressions on the document: doc.grand_total > 100000, doc.inspection_type == "Incoming".

Apply a transition in code — never set workflow_state directly:

from frappe.model.workflow import apply_workflow, get_transitions

apply_workflow(doc, "Approve")   # respects roles and conditions
get_transitions(doc)              # actions available to the current user

docs.title: Minimal working example — route inspections to the QA team
docs.text:
Desk → Assignment Rule → New, Document Type: Quality Inspection:

Field Value Assign Condition doc.inspection_type == "Incoming" Rule Round Robin Users qa.ahmed@…, qa.sana@…, qa.bilal@… Priority 1 Assignment Days Mon–Fri

Round Robin cycles through the users in order. Load Balancing gives the document to whoever has the fewest open assignments — the right choice for support tickets. Based on Field reads a User link field from the document itself (for example, each factory's designated auditor). The highest Priority rule that matches wins. Unassign Condition releases the assignment (for example, when the document is cancelled); Close Condition closes the ToDo when the work is done.

docs.title: When to use — and when not to
docs.text: Situation Use "Who may approve this, and in what order?" Workflow "Whose desk does this land on?" Assignment Rule A rule the document must pass (dates, quantities, limits) Controller validate / before_submit — not a Workflow condition A document that is never submitted No Workflow — workflows need a submittable DocType A one-off approval by email Share the document + a comment — not a whole Workflow Routing by team, territory, or workload Assignment Rule, not a Workflow state

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Intermediate state at docstatus 1. The document submits halfway through approval and can never go back to draft. Approvals stay at 0 until the final state.
  • Setting doc.workflow_state directly to skip an approval. Use apply_workflow — it checks roles, conditions, and self-approval.
  • Calling doc.submit() on a workflow-controlled document. The workflow does the submit, when the final transition runs.
  • Driving state with a custom Select field. Use the Workflow State field (workflow_state) — that is what the engine reads.
  • No state with docstatus 0. New documents start there. Without one, nothing can be created.
  • An Assignment Rule with no users, or a condition that never matches. Test the rule with a real document — an unmatched rule silently does nothing.
  • Two active workflows on one DocType. Only one can be active; the second activation deactivates the first.
  • Business validation in a transition condition. Conditions decide who may act; validation belongs in the controller (Lesson 05).

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
You have finished Level 2. You can put logic where it belongs, shape the form, expose an API, build a report and a print format, lock down who sees what, and route approvals to the right people.

Level 3 starts with the Scheduler — background jobs and queues: 11 — Scheduler & Background Jobs.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Two different things that beginners mix up:

  • The scheduler runs code on a clock — every hour, every day, at 2 AM. You register the work in scheduler_events in hooks.py. The scheduler does not run your code; it only enqueues it. A worker process picks it up from a Redis queue and runs it.
  • A background job runs code now, but not in the request. You start it with frappe.enqueue() — for example, when a user clicks "Generate report" and the report takes two minutes. The user gets an answer immediately; the work finishes in the background.

If either part is down — scheduler, workers, or Redis — nothing runs, and the user sees nothing. That is why "the job never ran" is a debugging question (Lesson 16), not a code question.

docs.title: Minimal working example — spice batch expiry check
docs.text:
Every morning, find spice batches expiring within 30 days and email the QA Manager. Scheduled work takes no arguments — the scheduler passes none.

# my_app/tasks.py
import frappe
from frappe.utils import add_days, today


def notify_expiring_batches():
    """Runs daily. No arguments — the scheduler passes none."""
    expiring = frappe.get_all("Batch",
        filters={
            "expiry_date": ("between", [today(), add_days(today(), 30)]),
            "disabled": 0,
        },
        fields=["name", "item", "expiry_date"])
    if not expiring:
        return
    rows = "\n".join(
        f"- {b['item']} ({b['name']}) expires {b['expiry_date']}"
        for b in expiring
    )
    frappe.sendmail(
        recipients=["qa.manager@nextash.example"],
        subject=f"{len(expiring)} spice batches expiring soon",
        message=f"The following batches expire within 30 days:\n\n{rows}",
    )

# hooks.py — registry only, no logic here
scheduler_events = {
    "daily": ["my_app.tasks.notify_expiring_batches"],
    "hourly_long": ["my_app.tasks.sync_supplier_stock"],
    "cron": {"0 2 * * *": ["my_app.tasks.nightly_archive"]},
}

Run bench --site <site> migrate after any change to hooks.py, or the scheduler never sees the new event.

Event key When Queue all Every tick (v15+: 60s) default — never more than 60s of work hourly / daily / weekly / monthly On the hour / day / week / month default (5 min timeout) hourly_long / daily_long / weekly_long / monthly_long Same times long (25 min timeout) cron Any cron expression, e.g. 0 2 * * * default unless you enqueue to long yourself

docs.title: Minimal working example — a long job from a button
docs.text:
A user submits a Sales Order and wants a stock-availability check across 3 warehouses. That takes minutes — it must not run inside the request:

# my_app/selling/api.py
import frappe
from frappe.utils.background_jobs import is_job_enqueued


@frappe.whitelist()
def check_stock_availability(sales_order):
    job_id = f"stock-check-{sales_order}"
    if is_job_enqueued(job_id):
        return _("Stock check already running for {0}").format(sales_order)
    frappe.enqueue(
        "my_app.selling.jobs.check_stock_availability",
        queue="long",
        timeout=1500,
        job_id=job_id,
        enqueue_after_commit=True,   # run only if the save commits
        sales_order=sales_order,      # simple values only — never a doc
    )
    return _("Stock check started — you will be notified when it finishes")

# my_app/selling/jobs.py
import frappe


def check_stock_availability(sales_order):
    """Runs in a worker. Handle its own errors — log, then re-raise."""
    order = frappe.get_doc("Sales Order", sales_order)
    # ... heavy warehouse checks, commit in batches ...
    # on failure: frappe.log_error(title=..., message=frappe.get_traceback())

Queues are short (quick jobs, under a minute), default (1–5 min), and long (heavy jobs, over 5 min, 25 min timeout). Always pass queue= explicitly — never rely on the default.

docs.title: Checking health
docs.text:
bench doctor                                        # workers + scheduler alive?
bench --site mysite enable-scheduler                # turn the scheduler on
bench --site mysite trigger-scheduler-event daily   # run one event by hand
bench --site mysite execute my_app.tasks.notify_expiring_batches  # or run the fn directly

Desk → Scheduler Log shows when each event last ran and whether it failed; failed jobs also write to the Error Log with the full traceback. On Frappe Cloud shared benches there is no shell — manage the scheduler from the dashboard.

docs.title: When to use — and when not to
docs.text: Situation Use Runs at a fixed time or interval scheduler_events in hooks.py Runs because a user did something frappe.enqueue() from the controller / API Work on one specific document frappe.enqueue_doc(doctype, name, method) Work over 5 minutes *_long event or queue="long" Work that must not run twice at once job_id= + is_job_enqueued() check Calling an external API on_submit / on_update + enqueue — never in validate A quick check the user waits for Run it in the request — no job needed

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Arguments on a scheduled function. The scheduler passes none — a def daily_cleanup(company): errors every tick.
  • A 20-minute job on the daily event. The default queue kills it at 5 minutes. Use daily_long or queue="long".
  • External API call in validate. The user waits, the API is slow, the save times out. Enqueue from on_submit instead.
  • Passing a document to enqueue. Jobs are serialised — pass names and IDs, then frappe.get_doc inside the job.
  • A job that is not idempotent. Running twice must not double-post or double-charge. Store the external ID on the document and check it.
  • No enqueue_after_commit. The job runs even if the save rolls back, on a document that was never saved.
  • Scheduler disabled on the dev site. bench new-site leaves it off — run enable-scheduler, or the job "never runs".
  • Swallowing errors in a job. A job that fails silently looks like a job that never ran. Catch, frappe.log_error, re-raise.
  • Forgetting bench migrate after editing hooks.py. The scheduler keeps running the old list.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: 12 — Notifications, Email & Integrations — telling people things happened: the Notification DocType, sending mail from code, and webhooks.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Three ways Frappe tells someone something happened, and one way it tells another system:

Way For Notification DocType No-code alerts on a document event — configurable by users, shipped as a fixture frappe.sendmail() Email from code, with full control over when and what frappe.publish_realtime() Live updates in the browser (the bell icon, a list refresh) Webhook DocType Frappe calls an external URL when a document event happens

Email is queued, not sent instantly: frappe.sendmail puts a row in the Email Queue, and the scheduler sends it. That is why mail needs a working scheduler (Lesson 11) and an Email Account with "Enable Outgoing" ticked.

docs.title: Minimal working example — Notification, no code
docs.text:
A Quality Inspection is rejected. The QA Manager and the person who created it must know. Desk → Notification → New:

Field Value Document Type Quality Inspection Event Value Change Value Changed status Condition doc.status == "Rejected" Channel Email Recipients By Role: Quality Manager; By Document Field: owner Subject Inspection {{ doc.name }} rejected Message Batch {{ doc.batch_no }} failed inspection. Reason: {{ doc.remarks }}

Events available: New, Save, Submit, Cancel, Value Change, Days Before, Days After, Method, Custom. "Days Before/After" runs on a date field — for example, remind the buyer 7 days before a supplier contract ends. Conditions are Python expressions on doc. Messages are Jinja — {{ doc.name }}, {{ doc.customer }}, any field on the document.

docs.title: Minimal working example — email from code
docs.text:
Same idea, but the logic decides who gets it. First add an approved_by Link field (Options: User) to the Gate Pass DocType — who approved this pass. Send from on_submit / on_update, never from validate — validation may still fail, and then you emailed about a document that was never saved.

# my_app/my_module/doctype/gate_pass/gate_pass.py
import frappe
from frappe import _


class GatePass(Document):
    def on_submit(self):
        frappe.sendmail(
            recipients=[self.approved_by],
            subject=_("Gate Pass {0} submitted").format(self.name),
            message=_(
                "Gate Pass {0} for visitor {1} was submitted by {2}."
            ).format(self.name, self.visitor_name, frappe.session.user),
            reference_doctype=self.doctype,   # links the mail in the timeline
            reference_name=self.name,
        )

Keep the default queueing. Never now=True in production — it sends inside the request, blocks the user, and on v16 it does not commit. Bulk mail (hundreds of customers) goes through frappe.enqueue first.

A reusable body lives in an Email Template — a templates/emails/order_approved.html file in your app, passed as template="order_approved", args={"doc": doc} instead of message=.

docs.title: Email Account setup
docs.text: Desk → Email Account → New: SMTP host/port and login for outgoing, IMAP for incoming. Tick Enable Outgoing to send, Enable Incoming to receive; incoming mail can create documents — set Append To to a DocType. If mail never arrives, check in order: outgoing enabled → Email Queue status and error → scheduler enabled (bench doctor) → mute_emails in site_config.json.

docs.title: Minimal working example — realtime + webhook
docs.text:
Tell the browser a long job finished (Lesson 11), and tell the warehouse system a Sales Order was submitted:

# inside the background job, when it finishes
frappe.publish_realtime(
    "stock_check_done",
    {"sales_order": order.name, "shortages": shortages},
    user=frappe.session.user,
)

// public/js/sales_order.js
frappe.realtime.on("stock_check_done", (data) => {
    frappe.msgprint(__("Stock check finished for {0}", [data.sales_order]));
});

Webhook — Desk → Webhook → New: Document Type Sales Order, Doc Event After Submit, the warehouse system's URL, Method POST, and a Jinja JSON body in Request Structure:

{"order": "{{ doc.name }}", "customer": "{{ doc.customer }}", "items": {{ doc.items | tojson }}}

Set a Webhook Secret in production. The receiver verifies the X-Frappe-Webhook-Signature header (HMAC-SHA256) to know the call really came from your site. Incoming webhooks are the mirror image: a whitelisted method that verifies the signature or token first, then enqueues the processing — never processes a webhook inside the request.

docs.title: When to use — and when not to
docs.text: Situation Use Alert on a doc event, users may change the rule Notification DocType Email from code with custom logic frappe.sendmail() Live UI update (bell, list refresh) frappe.publish_realtime() Another system must know an event happened Webhook DocType Bulk mail to hundreds of recipients frappe.enqueue + sendmail A one-off email to one person Share the document + a comment — no code

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• frappe.sendmail in validate. The save can still fail after the mail went out. Send from on_submit / on_update.
  • now=True in production. It blocks the request and, on v16, does not commit. Queue the mail and let the scheduler send it.
  • No Email Account with outgoing enabled. sendmail queues the mail, the queue never sends, and nobody notices for a week.
  • A Notification with no condition on a busy DocType. Every save of every Sales Order emails the whole team.
  • Secrets in a webhook URL or a Notification. Keys live in site_config.json or a Password field (Lesson 15), never in a URL.
  • No timeout on an external call. A hung supplier API hangs your worker. Always timeout=30, try/except, frappe.log_error.
  • Processing a webhook in the request. Verify, enqueue, return. The sender retries if you are slow, and you process it twice.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: 13 — Testing — proving the code works before the client finds out it doesn't: unit tests, test data, and UI tests.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A test proves a rule works — and keeps proving it every time someone changes the code later. Frappe tests are Python unittest tests that run against a real site and a real database. Each test runs inside a transaction that rolls back afterwards, so tests never leave data behind.

Test files live next to the DocType they test, and the file must start with test_ or the runner ignores it:

my_app/my_module/doctype/gate_pass/
    gate_pass.py
    test_gate_pass.py        # <-- tests live here
    test_records.json        # <-- optional test data
Version Needs DB? Base class v15+ no (pure logic) from frappe.tests.classes import UnitTestCase v15+ yes from frappe.tests.classes import IntegrationTestCase v14 any from frappe.tests.utils import FrappeTestCase

docs.title: Minimal working example — testing the Gate Pass rule
docs.text:
Lesson 05 put a rule in the Gate Pass controller: a Delivery/Pickup pass needs at least one item, and every row needs qty > 0. Test it:

# my_app/my_module/doctype/gate_pass/test_gate_pass.py
import frappe
from frappe.tests.classes import IntegrationTestCase


class TestGatePass(IntegrationTestCase):
    def test_delivery_pass_needs_items(self):
        doc = frappe.get_doc({
            "doctype": "Gate Pass",
            "purpose": "Delivery",
            "visitor_name": "Test Visitor",
            "items": [],
        })
        self.assertRaises(frappe.ValidationError, doc.insert)

    def test_zero_qty_is_rejected(self):
        doc = frappe.get_doc({
            "doctype": "Gate Pass",
            "purpose": "Delivery",
            "visitor_name": "Test Visitor",
            "items": [{"item_name": "Red Chilli Powder", "qty": 0}],
        })
        self.assertRaises(frappe.ValidationError, doc.insert)

    def test_valid_pass_saves_and_submits(self):
        doc = frappe.get_doc({
            "doctype": "Gate Pass",
            "purpose": "Delivery",
            "visitor_name": "Test Visitor",
            "items": [{"item_name": "Red Chilli Powder", "qty": 5}],
        })
        doc.insert()
        doc.submit()
        self.assertEqual(doc.docstatus, 1)

Test behaviour, not internals: validations throw, totals compute, submit/cancel work, permissions deny. A test that checks a private helper's return value breaks the moment someone refactors; a test that checks "a bad pass cannot be saved" survives.

docs.title: Test data and permissions
docs.text:
Create the data inside the test (as above), or put it in test_records.json next to the DocType — the runner loads it before the tests run. Never depend on production data: a test that passes on your machine and fails on the client's is worse than no test.

Check permissions the same way a user would hit them:

def test_warehouse_user_cannot_submit(self):
    frappe.set_user("warehouse.user@example.com")
    doc = frappe.get_doc("Gate Pass", "GP-0001")
    self.assertRaises(frappe.PermissionError, doc.submit)
    frappe.set_user("Administrator")   # always restore

Mock external HTTP calls with unittest.mock.patch. A test that calls a real supplier API is slow, flaky, and charges real money.

docs.title: Running tests
docs.text:
bench --site test.local set-config allow_tests true   # once, on the test site
bench --site test.local run-tests --app my_app
bench --site test.local run-tests --doctype "Gate Pass"
bench --site test.local run-tests --doctype "Gate Pass" --test test_zero_qty_is_rejected
bench --site test.local run-tests --app my_app --failfast

Use a separate test site, never production. The bench new-app scaffold generates a GitHub Actions workflow (.github/workflows/ci.yml) that creates a test site, installs the app, and runs the tests on every push — wire it up once and the tests run themselves.

docs.title: UI tests
docs.text:
Python tests prove the server logic. UI tests prove the form works the way a user uses it — a button appears, a field becomes mandatory, a list loads. Frappe uses Cypress: write .js specs in cypress/integration and run them against a running test site:

bench --site test.local run-ui-tests my_app            # opens the Cypress runner
bench --site test.local run-ui-tests my_app --headless  # CI mode

UI tests are slow and need a browser. Keep them for the handful of flows that must never break (login, create Sales Order, submit Quality Inspection) — everything else belongs in a Python test.

docs.title: When to use — and when not to
docs.text: Situation Use A validation, a total, a status change Python test, IntegrationTestCase Pure logic with no database UnitTestCase (v15+) — fast "Can this role do this?" Python test with frappe.set_user A critical user flow end to end Cypress UI test A rule you just fixed a bug in A test that fails without the fix — first "Does the button look right?" Look at it. Not everything needs a test

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• frappe.db.commit() inside a test. Each test rolls back. A commit breaks isolation and leaks data into the next test.
  • Depending on production data. The test passes on your laptop, fails on CI and on the client. Create data in the test.
  • Running tests on the production site. Tests insert, submit, and cancel documents. Use a disposable test site.
  • A test file not starting with test_. The runner silently skips it — zero tests run, zero failures, false confidence.
  • Calling real external APIs in tests. Mock them. A supplier API being down must not fail your test suite.
  • Forgetting to restore the user. frappe.set_user(...) without restoring to Administrator leaks the wrong user into later tests.
  • Only testing the happy path. The bug is always in the case you did not test: zero qty, missing customer, cancelled document.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: 14 — Performance — the report that takes 30 seconds and the submit that times out: N+1 queries, indexes, and caching.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: Slow Frappe code is almost always one of four things: too many queries, the wrong query, no index, or work done in the request that belongs in a background job. The fixes are small and mechanical — but only if you measure first. A report that takes 30 seconds has a cause you can find; guessing rewrites is how a 30-second report becomes a 40-second report.

docs.title: Minimal working example — the N+1 query
docs.text:
The big one. Never frappe.get_doc (or get_value) inside a loop to read one value — that is one database query per row.

# ❌ 200 items = 200 queries
for row in self.items:
    group = frappe.db.get_value("Item", row.item_code, "item_group")

# ✅ one query, then a dict lookup
item_codes = [row.item_code for row in self.items]
groups = dict(frappe.get_all("Item",
    filters={"name": ("in", item_codes)},
    fields=["name", "item_group"], as_list=True))
for row in self.items:
    group = groups.get(row.item_code)

Same rule for totals: aggregate in SQL, don't load rows into Python.

# ❌ loads every Stock Ledger Entry row
total = sum(e.actual_qty for e in frappe.get_all("Stock Ledger Entry",
    filters={"item_code": item_code}, fields=["actual_qty"]))

# ✅ the database sums
total = frappe.db.sql("""
    SELECT SUM(actual_qty) FROM `tabStock Ledger Entry`
    WHERE item_code = %s
""", item_code)[0][0] or 0

docs.title: Pick the right read
docs.text:
Need Use Why One field of one document frappe.db.get_value One cheap query A rarely-changing master (Company, settings) frappe.get_cached_value / frappe.get_cached_doc Served from Redis, no query A list the user may see frappe.get_list Permission-aware — respects roles A list for system code frappe.get_all Faster, but no permission check Just the names frappe.get_all(..., pluck="name") No dicts built A count or sum frappe.db.sql / frappe.qb aggregate The DB aggregates, Python doesn't

get_list vs get_all is a security decision as much as a speed one (Lesson 15): get_all returns rows the user is not allowed to see. Use get_list for anything user-facing.

docs.title: Caching — what rarely changes
docs.text:
Item groups, price lists, tax templates: read on almost every document, changed once a month. Cache them in Redis with a generator — the first call computes, later calls read the cache:

def get_item_group(item_code):
    return frappe.cache().get_value(
        f"item_group:{item_code}",
        generator=lambda: frappe.db.get_value("Item", item_code, "item_group"),
    )

Rules: cache shared, rarely-changing data under a key that names what it is. Never cache per-user data under a shared key — the next user gets the first user's answer. Invalidate when the source changes (clear the key in the DocType's on_update), or the cache serves yesterday's truth.

docs.title: Indexes
docs.text: A filter on a field without an index scans the whole table. Tick Search Index on DocType fields used in frequent filters — item_code on Stock Ledger Entry, customer on Sales Order, batch_no on Quality Inspection. Check a slow query with EXPLAIN in MariaDB before adding an index; an index on the wrong column helps nothing and slows writes.

docs.title: Reports and denormalizing
docs.text:
A Script Report that loads 10,000 rows and filters in Python is slow twice: once to fetch, once to filter. Filter in the query (frappe.db.sql with WHERE, or Query Builder), fetch only the fields the report shows, and paginate.

When a value is computed from many rows on every read — a customer's total outstanding, a batch's remaining qty — denormalize: store the computed value on the parent document and update it when the children change (in the controller, Lesson 05). Reads become one field lookup. The price is write complexity, so denormalize only values that are read far more often than they change.

docs.title: When to use — and when not to
docs.text: Situation Use A value read in a loop Bulk fetch once, dict lookup A count, sum, or average SQL aggregate, not Python A master read on every document get_cached_value / frappe.cache() A slow report Filter in SQL, fetch only shown fields Work over a few seconds frappe.enqueue (Lesson 11) A value read 100× more than written Denormalize onto the parent A one-off admin query Slow is fine — don't optimise it

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• get_doc in a loop. The single most common performance bug in Frappe apps. Bulk fetch and map.
  • get_all for user-facing reads. Fast — and leaks rows the user must not see. get_list for users, get_all for system code.
  • frappe.db.commit() inside a request. The framework commits. (Allowed only in long background jobs / patches, in batches.)
  • Calling the server from refresh for data that rarely changes. Load once in onload, or set frm.doc.__onload from the controller.
  • No index on the filtered field. The query is fast on 100 rows and dead on 100,000. Add search_index before the client grows.
  • Caching per-user data under a shared key. Every user sees the first user's data. Key by user, or don't cache it.
  • Optimising without measuring. Find the slow query first (Error Log, bench --site <site> console, EXPLAIN), then fix it.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: 15 — Security — the things that must never happen: injection, leaked data, guest endpoints that write, and secrets in code.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: Assume every input is hostile: form fields, URL parameters, file uploads, webhook payloads, imported rows. The framework gives you safe APIs — use them, don't work around them. Most security bugs in Frappe apps are not exotic attacks; they are a developer passing ignore_permissions=True "to make it work" and leaving it there.

docs.title: Minimal working example — a search endpoint, wrong and right
docs.text:
A customer portal needs to search items by name. The first version works — and lets anyone read any table:

# ❌ SQL injection + no permission check
@frappe.whitelist()
def search_items(q):
    return frappe.db.sql(
        f"SELECT name, item_name FROM `tabItem` WHERE item_name LIKE '%{q}%'"
    )

# ✅ parameterised, permission-checked, user-facing read
@frappe.whitelist()
def search_items(q):
    frappe.has_permission("Item", "read", throw=True)
    return frappe.get_list("Item",
        filters={"item_name": ("like", f"%{q}%")},
        fields=["name", "item_name"],
        limit_page_length=20)

Three fixes in one: the query is parameterised (frappe.get_list builds the SQL for you), the method checks the caller's permission before returning data, and the result is limited. Whitelisting does not check permissions for you — every @frappe.whitelist() method must do it itself.

SQL injection, stated plainly — never build SQL from user input:

Wrong Right frappe.db.sql(f"... where name='{user}'") frappe.db.sql("... where name=%s", user) "... where name='" + name + "'" frappe.qb.from_("User").select("*").where(Field("name") == name)

Placeholders work for values only. A table or column name from input can't be a placeholder — validate it against a fixed allowlist first.

docs.title: XSS — Jinja does not autoescape
docs.text:
Frappe renders Jinja in a sandbox, but it does not escape HTML. {{ doc.remarks }} in a print format, email, or web template renders raw HTML — including a <script> a user typed into a remarks field.

Wrong Right {{ doc.remarks }} in a print format {{ doc.remarks \| e }} {{ html \| safe }} on user content \|safe only on HTML your own code generated $(el).html(frm.doc.notes) in JS $(el).text(frm.doc.notes)

docs.title: Permissions — the rules that get broken
docs.text:
• ignore_permissions=True only with a comment explaining why — for example, a system-generated document in a method that already checked a business rule. Without the comment, the next developer copies it everywhere.
  • allow_guest=True only for truly public endpoints (signup, public page data). A guest method must never return private data or accept writes without its own validation. Rate-limit guest endpoints with @frappe.rate_limit.
  • frappe.get_list is permission-aware; frappe.get_all is not. User-facing reads use get_list (Lesson 14).
  • Don't trust request parameters for identity. Use frappe.session.user, never a user value from frappe.form_dict.
  • Hiding a field in JS is not security. Anyone can read it through the API. Use permlevel (field-level permission, Lesson 09).

docs.title: Secrets and API keys
docs.text:
Wrong Right API key in code, fixtures, or a committed JSON bench set-config <key> <value> — site_config.json is not in git Password in a Data field Password fieldtype — encrypted at rest; read with frappe.utils.password.get_decrypted_password Token in a Client Script / JS Keep it server-side; expose only via a whitelisted method that checks permission

Read site config with frappe.get_site_config() / frappe.conf. Never log secrets, never put them in error messages or test data. A leaked secret must be rotated immediately — deleting the file doesn't remove it from git history.

API access: create a dedicated API user with minimal roles, never use Administrator keys. Calls authenticate with Authorization: token <api_key>:<api_secret>. Rotate keys when someone leaves; a key that never expires is a key that never stops working.

docs.title: Files and audit
docs.text:
Uploads attached to documents are File docs with is_private. Private files need a logged-in user with permission on the attached document to download. Don't serve user files from public/, don't link a private file's file_url on a guest page, and validate uploads server-side before saving.

For audit: turn on Track Changes on sensitive DocTypes — every change is kept as a Version you can review. The Activity Log shows who did what and when. When something goes wrong, the first question is always "who changed this, and when?" — the logs must be able to answer it.

docs.title: When to use — and when not to
docs.text: Situation Use User input in a query Placeholders / frappe.qb / get_list filters User text in a template \| e escape; \|safe never on user content A system action the user can't do ignore_permissions=True + a comment, after a check A public page or form allow_guest, validate every input, show no internal data A secret, key, or token site_config or a Password field — never code or JS An external system calling in Dedicated API user, minimal roles, rotate keys

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• F-string SQL. The single most dangerous line in a Frappe app. One f"..." with user input and the whole database is readable.
  • ignore_permissions=True without a comment. It spreads. The next developer copies it because "it worked last time".
  • allow_guest=True on a method that writes. Guest endpoints are public. Anyone on the internet can call them.
  • Administrator API keys in an integration. One leaked key is full control. Dedicated user, minimal roles, rotated keys.
  • Secrets in git. A key committed once lives in history forever. Rotate it, then remove it — in that order.
  • Private files linked from a guest page. is_private means nothing if you hand out the URL.
  • "Hidden" fields as security. JS hiding and hidden fields are UX. The API returns what the DocType allows — use permlevel.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: 16 — Debugging — when it breaks anyway: reading a traceback, the logs, bench console, and the errors every Frappe developer meets.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Debugging is not guessing. It is: reproduce it, read what the system already told you, isolate the cause, fix it, prove it. Frappe tells you a lot — a traceback, an Error Log row, a worker log line — but only if you look in the right place instead of changing random code and hoping.

Read a traceback bottom-up. The last frame is where it failed; the frames above it are how it got there. The exception type on the last line is the diagnosis — DoesNotExistError and ValidationError are different problems with different fixes.

docs.title: Minimal working example — walking a real traceback
docs.text:
A user submits a Gate Pass and gets a 500 error. The Error Log shows:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "apps/frappe/frappe/model/document.py", line 1123, in submit
    self._submit()
  File "apps/my_app/my_app/my_module/doctype/gate_pass/gate_pass.py", line 42, in on_submit
    approver = frappe.get_doc("User", self.approved_by)
frappe.exceptions.DoesNotExistError: User HR-EMP-0042 does not exist

Read it bottom-up:

  1. Last line first — DoesNotExistError: User HR-EMP-0042 does not exist. The code asked for a User that isn't there.
  2. Your file, not Frappe's — gate_pass.py, line 42, in on_submit. The framework frames above it are just the call path.
  3. The cause — approved_by holds an employee ID, not a user email. The field was linked to the wrong DocType, or filled with the wrong value.
  4. The fix — validate the link (or use frappe.db.exists("User", self.approved_by) before get_doc), and fix the bad data.

docs.title: Where the evidence lives
docs.text:
Place Shows Error Log (Desk) Every unhandled exception, with the full traceback Activity Log (Desk) Who did what, when — for "it worked yesterday" bench --site <site> console A live Python shell on the site — inspect any doc, run any function logs/ in the bench folder web.log, worker.log, scheduler.log, bench.log bench doctor Are the workers and scheduler alive? (Lesson 11) bench --site <site> execute <dotted.path> Run one function by hand, outside any request 
# reproduce it in the console — faster than clicking through the form
bench --site mysite console
>>> doc = frappe.get_doc("Gate Pass", "GP-0007")
>>> doc.approved_by
'HR-EMP-0042'
>>> frappe.db.exists("User", "HR-EMP-0042")   # None — there it is

Log properly when you add logging. print() goes to a worker log nobody reads and vanishes on Frappe Cloud. Use the Error Log:

try:
    sync_supplier_stock()
except Exception:
    frappe.log_error(
        title="Supplier stock sync failed",
        message=frappe.get_traceback(),
    )
    raise

docs.title: Common errors and their real causes
docs.text: Error Real cause Fix DoesNotExistError (404) get_doc on a missing record, or a wrong API path frappe.db.exists() first; check /api/method/dotted.path ValidationError (417) A frappe.throw ran Fix the input or the rule — the message says which PermissionError (403) Missing @frappe.whitelist(), role, or User Permission Add the decorator / role / permission (Lesson 09) DuplicateEntryError (409) Unique / naming clash Check exists first; fix autoname / naming series LinkValidationError A Link points to a record that doesn't exist Create or validate the target LinkExistsError Delete blocked by linked documents Show the links; cancel/delete dependents first TimestampMismatchError Document changed since it was loaded Reload — doc.reload() / frm.reload_doc() MandatoryError A required field is empty Set it before insert/save ImportError: __import__ not found import in a Server Script Use frappe.utils.* (Lesson 05) CSRFTokenError Raw fetch call / stale session Use frappe.call() AttributeError: module has no attribute Wrong dotted path in hooks.py Match the function name and path exactly Change not visible Cache / assets / migrate clear-cache, bench build --app <app>, migrate Job never runs Worker or scheduler off bench doctor, enable-scheduler

docs.title: Asking for help — what to paste
docs.text:
When you ask someone (or an AI) for help, paste these four things — nothing else is needed, and without them nobody can help:

  1. The full traceback as text — not a screenshot, not "it shows an error". Copy it from the Error Log.
  2. What you were doing — "submitting Gate Pass GP-0007", one line.
  3. What you already tried — "checked approved_by, it's an employee ID, not a user".
  4. Versions — bench version output: Frappe, ERPNext, your app.

"My code doesn't work" with no traceback gets you guesses. A traceback with versions gets you an answer.

docs.title: When to use — and when not to
docs.text: Situation Use Something broke Reproduce it first — then read the traceback "It worked yesterday" Activity Log + git log — what changed? A value looks wrong bench console — inspect the live document A job failed Error Log + Scheduler Log (Lesson 11) A user reports an error Ask for the exact steps + the Error Log row You have a theory Test it in the console before editing code

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Guessing instead of reproducing. Changing code before you can make the error happen on demand. Reproduce first, always.
  • Reading the traceback top-down. The top is framework internals. The answer is at the bottom, in your file.
  • print() debugging in production. It goes nowhere useful. Use frappe.log_error with the traceback.
  • Fixing the data, not the bug. Deleting the bad Gate Pass hides the error for a week. Fix the link field that let it in.
  • Editing a submitted document to "fix" it. Cancel and amend (Lesson: guides/common-mistakes.md) — an edited submitted document and its ledger disagree forever.
  • Pasting a screenshot of a traceback. Text can be searched and copied. A screenshot can't.
  • Changing three things at once. You won't know which one fixed it — or which one broke the next thing.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
You have finished Level 3. You can schedule work and run it in the background, notify people and other systems, test what you built, make it fast, keep it secure, and find out why it broke when it breaks.

Level 4 starts with the no-code side of v16 — Studio and Flow: 17 — Studio & Flow.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Two v16.60 features that change who builds things:

  • Studio is a visual app builder, merged into the Framework. You assemble pages from blocks, bind them to Frappe data, and publish — no code. The app lives in the database as Studio App and Studio Page records, and can be exported into a standard Frappe app for git and deployment.
  • Flow is an AI assistant inside Desk (beta, v16.60+). You ask in plain language and it works on your site — answers questions about live data, creates records, drafts documents. It works with the permissions of the person asking, so it can never see or change more than they can. It uses your own AI provider keys.

Lesson 13 in the ERPNext path introduced both at feature level. This lesson is the hands-on version: build one mini-app, ask one question.

docs.title: Minimal working example — a Gate Pass mini-app in Studio
docs.text:
Reuse the Gate Pass DocType from Lesson 03 as the data source. Desk → search Studio → New Studio App:

Field Value App Name gate-pass-app Title Gate Pass Route gate-pass Home Page passes

Page 1 — the list. New Studio Page, route passes. Add a data resource of type Document List on DocType Gate Pass, then drag a table block onto the page and bind its rows to that resource (columns: name, visitor, company, date). This is the page the guard opens on a phone.

Page 2 — the form. New Studio Page, route new-pass. Add a data resource of type Document on DocType Gate Pass (new document), then drag form blocks bound to its fields: visitor name, company, purpose, items. Add a submit button that saves the document.

Preview both pages from the Studio toolbar, fix the layout, then Publish. The app is live at /gate-pass on your site. To ship it as code (git, other sites): turn on developer mode, open the app in Studio, click Export App, turn on Enable App Export, pick your Frappe app, and click Update — Studio writes it to apps/<your_app>/studio/<app_name>/.

docs.title: Minimal working example — one Flow question
docs.text:
Setup first (System Manager only): open /flow on your site, choose a provider (Anthropic, OpenAI, or a custom OpenAI-compatible server such as Ollama), paste its API key, click Connect, and pick the model new chats start with. Give users the Flow User role.

Then, anywhere in Desk, press Ctrl+I (Cmd+I on Mac) and ask:

"Which customers have overdue Sales Invoices, and how much is each one owed?"

Flow reads the live data and answers with the numbers — and only the customers the signed-in user is allowed to see. Ask it to act, and it will offer to: "Create a ToDo for the sales manager listing the three oldest overdue invoices." Read what it is about to do before you approve it — Flow can misread data, and an approved action is a real action (beta).

docs.title: When to use — and when not to
docs.text: Situation Use A small app that does not justify a developer Studio — visitor register, sample tracking, gate pass An analyst needs a form + list in a day Studio A question about live data ("which orders are late?") Flow A draft document or a first version of a record Flow, then verify A full module (Manufacturing, HR, Accounting) The module — Studio is for the gap around modules, not a replacement A rule that must always hold Controller code (Lesson 05), never Flow A production change on live data A human, with a backup — Flow drafts, people decide

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Building in Studio what belongs in a module. If the app is really Manufacturing or HR, use the module.
  • Trusting Flow's answer without checking. Verify the numbers against the report before acting on them.
  • No owner for the AI keys. Flow uses your own provider keys — decide whose account and budget they are before the pilot, not after the bill.
  • Skipping the permission check. Flow respects permissions, but the underlying roles must be right first — an over-permissioned user makes the AI over-informed.
  • A Studio app nobody can find. Publish it, then put it where people look: the Desktop, or a link from the module it belongs to.
  • Never exporting the app. A database-only app cannot go to git or to another site. Export it once it works.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: 18 — Insights — dashboards on live data, built in Desk: data source, query, chart, dashboard.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Insights turns live ERP data into dashboards — no exports, no stale spreadsheets. Since v16.60 the dashboards embed in Desk, where managers already work. Four pieces, in order:

Piece What it is Data Source Where the data lives: a DocType table, or an external database (MySQL, PostgreSQL, DuckDB, BigQuery) Query One question against the data — built visually (Source, Join, Filter, Group & Summarise) or in SQL Chart One visualisation of a query: Number, Bar, Line, Row, Table, Pie Dashboard Charts arranged on a grid, with filters — the page the manager opens Workbook The folder that holds a set of queries, charts and dashboards, with its own permissions

docs.title: Minimal working example — a sales dashboard in Desk
docs.text:
Open Insights in Desk. Everything below happens inside one Workbook.

1. Workbook. Click + New Workbook, name it Sales Overview.

2. Query. A new workbook starts with a query — pick the source table Sales Invoice. Then add operations in order:

Source:  Sales Invoice
Filter:  docstatus = 1  AND  posting_date is this month
Group:   by customer, Sum of grand_total

Save the query as Monthly Sales by Customer. A query is reusable — every chart below reads from it, so the logic lives in one place.

3. Charts. Click + New Chart twice:

  • Number chart "Revenue this month": the Sum of grand_total from the query — the one number on top.
  • Bar chart "Revenue by customer": customer on one axis, grand_total on the other.

4. Dashboard. Click + New Dashboard, name it Sales Overview. Drag the two charts from the left panel onto the grid — Number on the first row, Bar below it. Click Filter, add a filter on company, so a manager with two companies sees one at a time.

Open the dashboard tomorrow and the numbers are current — Insights queries run against live data, not a copy. Put the dashboard where it gets opened: link it from the Desktop or the Selling workspace.

docs.title: When to use — and when not to
docs.text: Situation Use "How are we doing this month?" Insights dashboard in Desk One question, many views One query, several charts A number the owner checks daily Number chart on the first row A one-off question for one user Report Builder or a saved list filter — not a dashboard A printed document (invoice, gate pass) Print Format (Lesson 08), not Insights Data that must be frozen at month end A report exported to file — a live dashboard moves

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Dashboards nobody opens. A dashboard buried three clicks deep is decoration. Put the one number that matters where people look.
  • One query per chart. Build the query once, chart it many ways. Ten copies of the same logic drift apart.
  • No filter on a multi-company dashboard. Every chart shows all companies mixed together. Add the company filter.
  • A chart for every question. Five charts that answer one question hide the answer. One chart, one question.
  • Sharing the workbook with everyone. Workbooks carry their own permissions — share with the roles that may see the data, not the whole site.
  • Trusting a chart without checking the query. A wrong filter makes a confident-looking wrong number. Read the query first.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: 19 — Website & Portal — the public side of Frappe: web pages, Web Forms, and the customer portal.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Frappe has two faces: Desk (the internal app, logged-in users, roles) and the Website (public pages anyone can open). The portal is the middle ground — logged-in customers who see only their own documents. Three building blocks:

Block For Web Page A static public page (About, Terms, a landing page) Web Form A public form that creates a document — no Desk access for the submitter Portal Logged-in customers seeing their own orders, invoices, tickets
